articles.title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis sentenced to 40 years to life over murder of Tupac Shakur
articles.summary: ‘You don’t get to take a man from his family … and just walk away from it,’ judge says as former gang leader sentenced

blocks.text: Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leader convicted of murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of rapper Tupac Shakur, has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.

“For three years, I’ve heard you say some variation of the same thing … ‘Yeah, I was involved in this. But I’m different. I’ve moved on. I got out of Compton. I’m a grandfather now,’” Judge Carli Kierny said Tuesday as she delivered the sentence.
“You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it.”
On 7 September 1996, Shakur was gunned down near the Las Vegas strip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later.
For decades, his murder remained unsolved and one of hip-hop’s most enduring mysteries. Davis is the only person to be convicted in connection to Shakur’s murder.

A confluence of several factors hindered the investigation. The code of silence within street culture made some witnesses averse to police cooperation. Las Vegas police were skeptical about leads from their Compton counterparts, given that the head of security for Shakur’s record label was a former Compton cop.

Orlando Anderson, a gangster and Davis’s nephew, was on law enforcement’s radar as the possible gunman. The night Shakur was killed, the young rap star got into an altercation with Anderson. Las Vegas police interviewed Anderson, but he was never arrested. Anderson later died in 1998.
But then, in 2023, Davis was arrested on a murder charge.
It was Davis’s own media tour, touting his status as one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, and a 2019 “tell-all” memoir that led to the breakthrough.

Davis had felt emboldened by a 2008 backdoor deal he brokered with police. He spoke candidly to investigators about Shakur’s shooting, who had actually been seeking information about the death of Christopher Wallace, known as Biggie Smalls or The Notorious B.I.G. Under a proffer agreement, Davis was not to face charges for any offenses he shared.
In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis wrote that he and a group of other men targeted Shakur and his entourage, seeking retribution for the scuffle with his nephew.
after newsletter promotion
The memoir and the interview became central to prosecutor’s case. They argued the details amounted to a confession and that his public remarks voided the proffer agreement.

During Davis’s murder trial, his defense team maintained that these details were embellished. They also argued, during the trial, that there was no physical evidence, such as a murder weapon, tying Davis to the Las Vegas slaying.
Ultimately, jurors sided with the state.
Attorneys for Davis have indicated they want to appeal the conviction.

articles.title: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby defends family's enrolment in $10-a-day child-care
articles.summary: NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in British Columbia's $10-a-day child-care program. Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit…

image.caption: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is fending off attacks from the B.C. Conservatives about his family's use of the provincial $10-a-day child-care program. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in British Columbia's $10-a-day child-care program. Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit from the program that they say is inaccessible to many low-income families.
Eby's family has accessed subsidized child-care program which Conservative opponents say is 'shocking'
B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in the provincial $10-a-day child-care program.
Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit from the program that they say is inaccessible to many low-income families.
In a post on X Monday, Eby said one of his children was already attending a child-care centre when it was designated as a $10-a-day site.
"When that occurred, we chose as a family to make a donation to that excellent facility," Eby said.
"We felt that we did not need that discount and we wanted to make sure that the child-care centre could provide other supports for families in the community."
Eby said his family will make a similar donation to the child-care centre for their youngest child who attends the same facility.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Eby would not specify the donation amount or if it was used as a tax write off.
"We certainly didn't need that discount," Eby said.
"We paid the difference between what it was before and what it was after the $10-a-day daycare," he added.

items: More stories from Vancouver Island

blocks.text: Now, Eby is taking heat from the B.C. Conservatives during the snap provincial election campaign.

"It's shocking to learn that while hundreds of thousands of British Columbians are struggling with the most expensive child care in the country, David Eby's family landed a plum $10-a-day child care spot," said Margareta Dovgal, the B.C. Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Yaletown, in a news release Monday.

The Conservatives called attention to Eby's compensation from 2025 to 2026 as premier, which totalled more than $226,000, and criticized his "wealthy family" for benefiting from the subsidized child-care program.
After Eby's Tuesday news conference, Dovgal said Eby was dodging the tough questions.

"David Eby should look a working single mother paying thousands in childcare costs in the eye explaining why his wealthy, powerful family deserves $10/day childcare first," Dovgal said in a second news release.
"David Eby is trying to defend the indefensible, as British Columbians are seeing Eby for the opportunistic hypocrite he is."

The Conservatives are demanding Eby answer a number of questions, including around the value and proof of his first donation, whether it was a tax write-off, and more information on the value of the second planned donation.
What is the $10-a-day child-care program?

The $10-a-day program is operated by independent businesses who have chosen to participate; access to one of the facilities is based on each location's licensed capacity and waitlist, according to the provincial government.
When a child-care centre is approved to be a part of the $10-a-day program, the child's space is automatically converted into the $10-a-day program, according to a provincial Q&A webpage.

According to the webpage, which was last updated in 2024, there were more than 13,200 $10-a-day child-care spaces throughout B.C. The Ministry of Education and Child Care would not provide an updated number of spaces as the government is in a temporary caretaker mode due to the election.
The B.C. NDP say their Conservative opponents "have been silent" around whether their party would reverse child care fee caps.
Eby said Tuesday the Conservatives are proposing to cut certain child-care programs. However, the Conservatives have not laid out their plan yet.
CBC News has reached out to the B.C. Conservatives for their child-care proposals.

articles.title: Saudi coalition strikes fuel depot near Yemen's capital
articles.summary: The Houthis have warned Saudi Arabia that they will retaliate by targeting the Saudi cities of Riyadh and Dammam.

blocks.text: The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen has carried out a strike on fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility to fuel their war effort, including by supporting missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The coalition earlier warned civilians to evacuate the site ahead of a "special operation", with Houthi media saying the facility had been struck before al-Maliki confirmed the strike.
The Houthis have warned they will retaliate by targeting the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.

The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.

A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".

The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

articles.title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
articles.summary: The sentence marks an end to the mystery around Tupac's cold case, which has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

blocks.text: The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.

In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.
Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.

But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.
Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.
For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.
Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.
Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

articles.title: Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal
articles.summary: Germany's Johann Wadephul said hybrid plots like the Starlink fire showed Europe was "in Russia's crosshairs." The UK's Ed Miliband said Trump's Russian diesel deal led to a "very difficult few days"…

image.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said sanctions should continue being imposed on Russia's economy as attacks on Ukraine persistImage: Jörg Blank/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.

This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap.
What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.
"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.
"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.

blocks.caption: Germany's Johann Wadephul, Poland's Radoslaw Sikorski, Norway's Espen Barth Eide and the UK's Ed Miliband shared a stage at the Warsaw Security Forum on TuesdayImage: Dominik Butzmann/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things.

"Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor, and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said.
Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions.

"I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said.

Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements.

blocks.caption: The first two Starlink arrests took place in the small German town of Nürtingen in the southwest, far from Poland's bordersImage: Enrique Kaczor/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia
Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month.

Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia.
Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs."
The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeted accessibility across the border in the warzone.
"We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," he said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation."
But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels.
He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies.
A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them.

blocks.caption: Miliband and Sikorski, who spent many of his younger years in the UK, also held a joint press conference in Warsaw on TuesdayImage: Neil Milton/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea

UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.

However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.
"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said.
Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.
Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa.

"This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said.
Trump announces 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine war

articles.title: Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump’s diesel deal with Russia?
articles.summary: Donald Trump plans to allow the purchase of Russian diesel, drawing criticism at home and abroad. What is behind the US president’s decision and what should Ukraine do next? DW spoke with experts.

image.caption: Gas prices are on the rise in the USImage: Patrick T. Fallon/AFP

blocks.text: The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."
The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.

"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."
From the Oval Office to Miami
This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."

The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.

blocks.caption: Memories are rekindled of the February 2025 spat between Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Donald Trump and JD VanceImage: Jim Lo Scalzo/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.

"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."
Is Trump looking for a 'scapegoat?'

All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.
Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.

"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.
Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."

Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
How can the crisis be resolved?
Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.

"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.

At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.
Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.
"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.

Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.
Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.
"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.
What will change after November 3?

The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.

Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.

"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.
He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: ‘There was a chance to stop him’: Parents react with fury to paedophile nursery worker revelations
articles.summary:
More than 50 families call for investigation into how Vincent Chan was allowed to return to job after inquiry by nursery

The parents of the victims of paedophile nursery worker Vincent Chan…

blocks.text: The parents of the victims of paedophile nursery worker Vincent Chan have reacted with fury to the news that he was cleared to return to work after “significant concerns” were raised by the parent of a young girl.

As first revealed in the Guardian, Chan was reported to his employer, the nursery chain Bright Horizons, by a concerned parent in 2021. After being investigated by Bright Horizons, with the knowledge of Camden council, Chan was cleared to return to work at the nursery on the Finchley Road in north-west London. A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself abusing three-year-old girls in his care.
“I feel a level of anger that I can barely put into words,” said one mother. Images of her daughter were found on Chan’s personal devices after his arrest.

She added: “In 2021, around the time serious concerns had been raised about Vincent Chan, he was made my daughter’s key worker. We trusted him with her most intimate care, believing she was safe. Knowing there was a chance to stop him before he had such extensive access to her is unbearable. I am heartbroken, but above all furious at Bright Horizons for failing to protect our children.”

The families have called for an immediate “independent examination” of how the 2021 complaint was handled. In a statement issued by the law firm Leigh Day, which is representing 50 families affected by Chan’s abuse, they called for a “full and independent account of what happened, who knew what, when they knew it and why these decisions were made”.

The parents of Chan’s victims have been promised answers in the form of a repeatedly delayed safeguarding review, led by an independent reviewer appointed by Camden council. But many expressed fury that they only learned the review had been pushed back to 2027 in the Guardian article.

“Expressions of regret are meaningless,” said the parents in a statement. “Families deserve the truth about what happened, accountability for the decisions that were made, and action to make sure this cannot happen again. We cannot wait until 2027 for answers.”

The families also restated their calls for Camden council to consider prosecuting Bright Horizons under health and safety legislation. “The Guardian’s report also strengthens the case for a criminal investigation,” they said.

The row over the decision to clear Chan to return to work has overshadowed the Labour MP Sagal Abdi-Wali’s first week as an MP after her byelection victory in Holborn and St Pancras last week. Before becoming an MP, Abdi-Wali was leader of Camden council, presiding over the delayed review.

Earlier on Tuesday Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for Hampstead and Kilburn, wrote to Camden council, asking it to commit to publishing the documentation relating to the 2021 investigation. “These revelations are causing significant distress to parents in my constituency, particularly the families directly affected by Chan’s crimes,” Siddiq wrote.
Families should not have to wait any longer for these answers,” she added.

Camden council said: “We know the parents of the children who attended the nursery, and the wider public, will be concerned that a complaint was made about Vincent Chan to Bright Horizons in 2021 – and will want to know how this was responded to.

“In 2021, Camden council’s local authority designated officer (LADO) provided advice to Bright Horizons, after Bright Horizons informed them (the LADO) of a complaint. We have shared all relevant documents and information with the independent review team. We want families to get the answers they deserve, in full, through the outcome of the independent review.”
A Bright Horizons spokesperson said: “We remain appalled by Vincent Chan’s crimes, and our thoughts are first and foremost with the children and families affected.

“We strongly encourage parents to share all their concerns with the child safeguarding practice review (CSPR), which is being led by an independent reviewer and will rightly examine this case in full.
“As the review is ongoing, we are unable to comment without the express written authorisation of the committee.”

articles.title: Cardinal Tagle to preside over Mass on Wednesday as Pope Leo recovers from surgery
articles.summary: Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle will preside over a Mass in St. Peter"s Square on Wednesday, October 14, in place of Pope Leo XIV, as the pontiff recovers from surgery and a subsequent hospital…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 2:37am

Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle will preside over a Mass in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday, October 14, in place of Pope Leo XIV, as the pontiff recovers from surgery and a subsequent hospital stay.

The Vatican said Tagle, the pro-prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization, will lead the celebration at 10 a.m. (Vatican time) to be attended by participants in a Church meeting, including heads of Eastern Churches, presidents of bishops’ conferences, married couples and experts.
The Mass will include prayers for the Pope’s health and for families, Jesuit priest Giacomo Costa said at a Vatican briefing.
Tagle was recently approved by Leo as dean of the College of Cardinals, becoming the first Asian cleric selected for the position.

The dean of the college of cardinals is considered the "first among equals" among the Church's highest-ranking clerics and is responsible for taking charge of the secretive conclave process, held in the Sistine Chapel, once a pope dies or resigns.

The dean, elected by his peers and approved by the pope, serves a five-year term that can be renewed once, according to Church law. The role has mostly been filled by Europeans, but was held by the late Beninese Cardinal Bernardin Gantin from 1993-2002.

Tagle is seen as a close ally of Pope Francis and is known for an infectious smile and is sometimes called by his diminutive nickname "Chito". He leads the Vatican's Dicastery for Evangelization, effectively the Church's missionary arm.

Following his election, Cardinal Tagle will assume the title of the Suburbicarian Church of Ostia while retaining the title of the Suburbicarian Church of Albano.—With a report from Reuters/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Cornell suspends all frat parties as alleged gang rape fuels continued calls for action
articles.summary: Cornell University has suspended all frat parties and events for the rest of the 2026-27 academic year, president Michael Kotlikoff announced Tuesday, as an alleged gang rape at one of the school's…

image.caption: Cornell University students take part in a seven-hour sit-in on campus, in Ithaca, N.Y. on Monday, representing the seven hours over which a woman alleges she was sexually assaulted by university frat members in 2024. (Angelina Katsanis/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Cornell University has suspended all frat parties and events for the rest of the 2026-27 academic year, president Michael Kotlikoff announced Tuesday, as an alleged gang rape at one of the school's fraternities continues to fuel calls for action and accountability.
'Zero tolerance' for violating new directive, university president says
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 13, 2026 2:32 PM EDT | Last Updated: 28 minutes ago
Kotlikoff, who has faced pressure to resign over the case, said there would be "zero tolerance" for any violations of the new directive.
"Any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension," he said in a written statement posted on Cornell's website.
It's among a series of measures Kotlikoff said the university is taking "to strengthen campus safety, better support survivors, and begin addressing the social context of sexual violence at Cornell."
The case has drawn international media attention after a woman filed a lawsuit last month against the university and her alleged assailants.
The high-profile Cornell 7 case has sparked a conversation about sexual violence
The woman, referred to as Jane Doe in court documents, has accused seven members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity of raping her at the frat house in October 2024, while she was incapacitated.
The case set off a wave of protests, including on the university campus in Ithaca, N.Y., and calls for justice and, more broadly, an end to sexual violence.

items: What to know about the case of the 'Cornell 7'
Alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' Cornell president says
Creating a culture of consent on university campuses

blocks.text: Earlier this month, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Letitia James, the state's attorney general, as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.

Cornell also said last week that it had appointed Sally Yates, a former U.S. deputy attorney general, to review how the school "prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus."
That includes a review of how the university responded to Doe's allegations, it said.
Students march at UBC in support of alleged Cornell University gang-rape victim

In Tuesday's statement, Kotlikoff said the university would appoint a dedicated case manager to help individuals who report sexual misconduct navigate processes such as housing and academic accommodations.
Kotlikoff also said Cornell would allow criminal investigators from the New York State Police, who are independent of the university, to investigate sex assault allegations on campus.
Campus police, who have full law enforcement powers but are controlled by the university, generally investigate crimes reported on Cornell's campus.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Cornell bans all fraternity parties over gang sex assault allegations
articles.summary: The school has faced an uproar over how it handled assault allegations brought by a woman known as Jane Doe.

blocks.text: "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.

Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.
In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".
"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.
Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.
The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.

Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.

items: Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults

blocks.text: The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.
These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.
Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.

Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.

State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.

Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".
He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

articles.title: California coastal homes battered and bruised after weekend of intense waves and flooding
articles.summary:
Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected

Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a…

blocks.text: Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.

The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.
Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse.

At least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, the Long Beach Post reported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet.

blocks.caption: Waves from tropical storm Rachel destroy beachfront houses - loop

blocks.text: Further south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets.
By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water.

In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service.

The extreme weather comes as El Niño is supercharging the Pacific, leading to large and long-lasting storms. The last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5.
Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach, who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press that the last month has been “berserk”.
“This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” he said.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into homes and a sea wall in Long Beach. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images

blocks.text: California is bracing for a challenging winter with severe storms thanks to an exceptionally strong El Niño. Models from the the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) show a high chance this could be a historic El Niño and deliver rainy wet weather, landslides and destructive high tides.

The state is one of the places expected to be significantly affected by the climate pattern, although the effects are expected to be seen worldwide, with temperature spikes and rising global food prices.
Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Far-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AI
articles.summary:
Annual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for Britain

MI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious.…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: MI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious. The terror threat has become more diverse, with far-right anti-migrant threats on the rise; while Iran has now firmly emerged alongside Russia as a country seeking to undertake violent and deadly plots in the UK.

“There is no law of physics dictating that rising state threats will be accompanied by diminishing terrorist threats,” MI5’s director general, Ken McCallum, said, although one of his core messages was that people and the country at large needed to focus on being more resilient. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested.”

A key issue highlighted by McCallum was that years of anti-migrant, anti-Muslim hostility had now led to an increase in cases where people were “tipping into terrorist intent” – that is crossing the line from rhetoric to violence. It is a complex area, but one certainly fuelled by political hate narratives and online subcultures.

It is also fuelled by toxic rhetoric from abroad. Authoritarian regimes, McCallum said, were investing heavily “in trying to distort and divide our society” – although he was too polite to mention that there is plenty of evidence that voices from the US led by X owner Elon Musk are keen to sow division in the UK too, as they post about flashpoint events such as the June rioting in Belfast and Southampton.

blocks.caption: MI5 director general, Ken McCallum. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA

blocks.text: A second trend is that seemingly far-off conflicts, such as the wars the UK did not start in Ukraine or Iran, have a habit of rippling back home. It is less than eight months since the US and Israel attacked Iran, subsequently with a little help from Britain, but already Iran is trying to direct terror plots in the UK.

Both MI5 and the counter-terror police may have to do a little better to explain precisely what five men from London were doing in a village next to RAF Fairford in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, given that nothing of significance was found in the vans and nobody has been charged.

But McCallum warned that Iran had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites” – a likely reference to Fairford. That came a day after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind the episode. It would be surprising if both were wrong.

That is not the only possible example. At the beginning of October, two Iranians from Liverpool and Salford, were charged, accused of trying to make a chlorine powder bomb to target Jewish sites in Manchester. Prosecutors alleged they were directed by a third party, believed to be in Iran. The two have not yet pleaded to the charges; a trial at the Old Bailey is scheduled.

Yet, if these fast emerging threats were not enough, the normally sober McCallum decided to reference AI. He warned that AI could refine terror plots, supercharge hackers, produce individually targeted propaganda – and even help develop a novel bioweapon. This he added, with emphasis, was a subject on which they were “particularly focused,” as if it was episode one of a TV thriller.

While concerns were recently raised about scientists who have used AI to design viruses as Anthropic warned of five examples of scientists who had used Claude for researching novel pathogens, both instances provoked a scientific debate as to what is actually possible. And what McCallum did not mention was that AI is also an extraordinary and potentially intrusive tool for MI5 to seek out threat.

There is already enough for the intelligence agencies to think about, as the MI5 review makes clear: a country made more dangerous by blowback from strongmen starting what they think will be short wars; a rising tide of hatred that may start online but is morphing into violent intent in real life; a complex cocktail of external and internal threats that could have real-life consequences.
As McCallum himself recognised: “The protection of democracy – its institutions, its representatives, its principles – has never felt more vital.”

articles.title: Argentina lodges legal claim against UK's Falklands oil exploration
articles.summary: The action filed with an international maritime tribunal is the latest development in an escalating row over the Falkland Islands.

blocks.text: The Argentinian government has begun legal action seeking to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands in an escalating row with the UK.
Buenos Aires said in a statement the request lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea aimed to block activity authorised "illegally" by the UK.
The claim comes a fortnight after Argentinian President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies.
UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran criticised the "escalating campaign" from Argentina against companies operating in the Falklands, while announcing new protections for them.

The developments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the self-governing British territory, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentinian forces which had invaded the territory.
Earlier last month Milei also threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands.
Uma Kumaran accused the Argentinian government of "economic coercion" against the people of the Falkland Islands.
"We will do whatever it takes to support them," she told the House of Commons on Tuesday.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain.
The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom".
In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.
But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government.
While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary.

Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease".
The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly.
They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity.

They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion."
The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".
On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory".

Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.
UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year.

articles.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, resigns after reports alleging corruption
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she'll "vigorously defend" herself.

image.caption: Kimberly Guilfoyle is shown in Athens on Oct. 7. She was confirmed by the U.S. Senate as ambassador to Greece in September 2025. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
U.S. President Donald Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she'll "vigorously defend" herself.
The Wall Street Journal reported questionable conduct and possible corruption by Guilfoyle, which she denies

Trump's administration said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
"She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving on a trip to campaign for congressional Republicans.

In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle denied the allegations on Tuesday and vowed to "vigorously defend my name, my reputation and my integrity."

"I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right and defending the values that make America exceptional," she said. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

Guilfoyle, 57, lasted just over one year in the role, having been narrowly confirmed by the Senate in a vote that hewed close to party lines. Democrats doubted her qualifications and said the appointment smacked of patronage, as Guilfoyle had dated and once been engaged to Donald Trump Jr.

Greek, U.S. opposition parties want more info
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her.

"This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity," Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated "the same way as every other ambassador" and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.
On Capitol Hill, a number of Democrats serving on House and Senate committees have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle's tenure.

items: Hoekstra's missteps in Canada are mild compared to some of Trump's ambassadors

blocks.text: The Wall Street Journal's first report said Guilfoyle had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While in Greece last week, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio berated journalists for asking about the allegations.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," said Rubio.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 US credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.

The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the department's travel regulations."
The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, at her first media briefing Tuesday morning, said Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."

Trump-aligned ambassadors and diplomats in his second term have ruffled feathers in a handful of countries, including Canada, where a series of provocative comments made by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra led to a petition signed by tens of thousands of Canadians calling for his removal.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia strikes strategic oil depots near Yemen capital
articles.summary:
Civilians warned to evacuate outskirts of Sana’a ahead of biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure

Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital Sana’a, in a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.

Before the attack on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population ahead of the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.

The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often holds substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.

Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed to immobilise the Houthi army as it continues its push South including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.

The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday, that killed 13 and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.

A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.
The difference between the threats is that Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.

Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.
But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.

blocks.caption: A map released by the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition shows the targeted site of the Yemeni Oil Company and Al-Sabaha Central Station in Sana'a. Photograph: @CJFCS.

blocks.text: Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.

The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.

This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.
Government aligned forces sent reinforcement to the south west district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.

But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to seccede from the country’s north.

On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project”, – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.
Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.

Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.

articles.title: Iran seeking 'harder targets' for attacks abroad, UK warns
articles.summary: The warning from the head of the UK's domestic security agency comes after PM Burnham said an attempted plot at an air force base hosting US bombers was "almost certainly" coordinated in Tehran.

image.caption: The head of MI5 said more than 50 people have been arrested in 'Iran-linked operations' this yearImage: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The leader of the UK's MI5 domestic security service on Tuesday said that Iran is expanding the scope of the hybrid attacks that it coordinates in the UK and elsewhere.
In an annual address outlining his assessment of threats to the UK, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said a "major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites."

The remarks come after the US removed about a dozen long-range bombers from Fairford air base in the southern UK last week following an incident on September 27 during which several men were arrested on "suspicion of terrorism offenses." An investigation is ongoing.
Uptick in 'Iran-linked operations'
McCallum said these kinds of incidents were "not unique," warning that Tehran is seeking targets beyond Iranian diaspora living abroad who oppose the regime.
These include Iranian media organizations, Israeli interests in the UK, and arson attacks on Jewish sites that British authorities say were carried out by Iranian proxies.
The spy chief warned of an "unflinching response" to "those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets – whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas."
He added that more than 50 people have been arrested in "Iran-linked operations" in the UK over the past year.

However, McCallum said Iran's ability to carry out more severe and complex attacks using explosive drones remains limited by the sophistication of the proxies and criminals it has used ⁠for operations in the UK.

blocks.caption: An Iran-linked group claimed responsibility for an arson attack on a synagogue in AprilImage: Amanda Rose/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: UK says Fairford air base incident likely coordinated by Iran
On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the suspected plot at Fairford air base was coordinated in Iran and was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC).

The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited. Seven suspects are currently released on bail under strict conditions pending the investigation

Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment the day of the incident, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the "suspicious vehicles" that were reported near the base. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.

blocks.caption: Authorities were alerted to a 'suspicious vehicle' near RAF Fairford in GloucestershireImage: Ben Birchall/PA Wire/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."
He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.

Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."
Tehran has accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident, along with other accusations of coordinating attacks in the UK.

RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

articles.title: At least 160,000 people take to streets in third week of French school protests
articles.summary:
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joins teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools

More than 160,000 schoolchildren, students and trade unionists have…
articles.byline: Jon Henley and Angelique Chrisafis in Paris

blocks.text: More than 160,000 schoolchildren, students and trade unionists have marched in cities across France as protests over high school education continued into a third week and many demonstrators denounced policing tactics.

Riot police fired teargas at the end of Tuesday’s marches in Nantes and near the Montparnasse area of Paris, but most of the demonstrations over teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling school buildings held in cities including Lyon, Lille and Marseille were peaceful.
The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg joined an early morning protest outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
“Young people are not being included in the conversation,” said Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis.

As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils after accusations of police brutality, Thunberg said: “Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.”

blocks.caption: ‘Young people are not being included in the conversation,’ said Thunberg. Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Students outside the high school said Thunberg had encouraged them to continue with peaceful demonstrations.

The protests – backed by trade unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt.
France’s interior ministry said 161,500 people had turned out across the country on Tuesday, while similar marches drew more than 260,000 last Tuesday and 75,000 on Thursday.

“They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them,” the university students’ union UE – many of whose members are also demonstrating in solidarity, with an estimated 90% of France’s universities disrupted on Tuesday – posted on social media. High schools in Paris, Marseille and elsewhere were again blockaded.
French authorities hope the protests, some of which have resulted in violent clashes with riot police, will peter out during the two-week half-term school holiday that starts this weekend.

blocks.caption: Police use water cannon in an attempt to disperse protesters in Paris on Tuesday.  Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: Louis Létoublon of the student organisation Les Lycéens! said the protest movement had begun in deprived areas outside Paris where families were unable to afford holidays, so the autumn school vacation would not dampen anger.
“We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging,” Naouel, a high school student in Brest, told Agence France-Presse.
Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, said: “Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don’t get it.”
France is braced for more nationwide protests on Saturday, which could be joined by people angry at rising fuel and energy prices as well as the cost of living.

Jérôme Rodrigues, a high-profile member of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) protest movement in 2018 and 2019, was present at the Paris march on Tuesday, and there was speculation that gilets jaunes could return to the streets on Saturday.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: People march in Rennes on Tuesday. Photograph: Jeremías González/AP

blocks.text: “There is a lot of anger,” Rodrigues told journalists. He said people felt the government had not answered their concerns, offering only “crumbs” – whether on fuel prices or demands for more funding for schools.
Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “Our youth is determined …While there is no answer to demands, the mobilisation will continue.”

The education minister, Édouard Geffray, who has said 3,000 substitute teachers are being deployed in schools facing the most severe staff shortages, said on Tuesday that 214 of the country’s 3,700 high schools were completely closed.

French media have reported, however, that at least some classes have been cancelled or disrupted in many more schools, and some lycées – for pupils mostly aged between 15 and 18 – have switched wholly or partly to online learning.

The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called for restraint on Monday, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”, as government figures showed more than 6,800 people – mainly minors – had been detained during the protests.

About 1,500 people are being prosecuted, the justice ministry has said, while 24 allegations of police brutality against demonstrators are under investigation. More than 200 teenagers, 100 school staff and 700 police officers have been injured.

One young protester lost a hand from a police stun grenade, prompting the government to ban their use during the protests, while another lost the use of an eye and a third many of his teeth from a teargas canister fired at close range.
Rights groups and students have accused the police of a disproportionate use of force.
The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, defended the policing. “When demonstrations take place peacefully, there is no police intervention,” he said.
Six months from a crucial presidential election to replace Macron, rival politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests.

The far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, has highlighted the damage to schools and called for parents ⁠to foot repair bills, while her radical-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.

articles.title: Quebec author accused of using AI admits past plagiarism but maintains novel is his own work
articles.summary: After spending the last few weeks quietly watching his reputation be torn apart, Quebec-based author Thélyson Orélien is speaking out and addressing the allegations that he used artificial…

image.caption: Haitian-born Quebec writer, poet and novelist Thélyson Orélien poses for pictures during a photo session in Paris on Sept. 8, 2026. (Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Montreal

After spending the last few weeks quietly watching his reputation be torn apart, Quebec-based author Thélyson Orélien is speaking out and addressing the allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel.
'The experience I am going through is cruel,' says Thélyson Orélien in new statement
"It is slander and heresy," he wrote in a statement distributed Tuesday by his Quebec publishing house, Éditions du Boréal.
C'était ça ou mourrir, which translates to "It was either that or die," tells the story of a Haitian migrant who leaves his home for Canada, much like Orélien did following the 2010 earthquake.

The novel was lauded by many in the French-language literary world until an anonymous X account ran excerpts through an AI detection tool and publicly shared those screengrabs on Sept. 21 — the same day the novel won the Prix du roman Fnac.
According to the tool Pangram, the novel was "100 per cent" the work of generative AI.

In Tuesday's statement, Orélien says he used AI tools "here and there" for research, particularly when it comes to foreign idioms, but he says the text, structure and plot all come "straight from my gut."
He says for the past few weeks, he's been subject to a "lynching" through the media and racist harassment, which he says has been unbearable.
"The experience I am going through is cruel," he wrote in French.
"By attributing to a machine a text that is mine, that belongs to all my people, they have challenged not only my status as a writer but my humanity."
Award-winning Quebec author accused of using AI for bestselling book
In his statement, he also seemingly discredits the experts who have largely praised Pangram for its reliability and accuracy in detecting AI.

As the debate around the tool and Orélien's writing swirled, the author was accused of plagiarism for various columns dating back to 2012 for newspapers like La Presse. Those accusations became the clincher for different literary festivals and prizes, like the Prix Goncourt, which then distanced themselves from Orélien.
French columnist Samuel Fitoussi has since come out as one of five people behind the X account that made the initial allegation.

items: Was this award-winning book written by AI? Scandal deepens skepticism in literary world

blocks.text: Author calls his plagiarism a 'youthful indiscretion'
Where the allegations of plagiarism are concerned, Orélien admitted to it in some of his earlier work, saying on Tuesday they were "unacceptable" mistakes from his youth.
An avid reader, he says he was in a "hurry" to write after leaving Haiti. There were authors whose style captivated him, he says.
"I admired rhythms, ways of phrasing sentences that would stay in my head for days," he said. "But admiration did not give me the right to take — to claim as my own — texts that were not mine."
Thélyson Orélien's debut novel, C'était ça ou mourir, tells the story of a man who undertakes a journey across the Americas to escape gang violence in Haiti. (AFP via Getty Images)
Orélien says he's now asking that C'était ça ou mourrir be judged for what it is, saying it was inspired by his own lived experience and conversations he's had with migrants over the years.
"A youthful indiscretion cannot serve as evidence against a novel begun in 2017 that was finally published in 2026," he said.
"I didn't write this book to win awards or to become famous. I have nothing to prove to the people who accuse me."

items: Canadian websites take down articles written by suspected fake, AI-generated persona

blocks.text: Orélien was in the midst of a press tour in France when the scandal broke, and media outlets are reporting he has since returned to Quebec.
Éditions du Boréal says the author won't comment further on the matter and will not be doing any interviews, for now.

C'était ça ou mourrir is still in the running for the Prix Renaudot, considered the second most prestigious French literary award after the Prix Goncourt, as well as the Prix littéraire de la Porte Dorée and the Prix Médicis.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Cassandra Yanez-Leyton is a journalist for CBC News based in Montreal. You can email her story ideas at cassandra.yanez-leyton@cbc.ca.
