articles.title: India: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?
articles.summary: Thousands detained, leaders arrested on arrival, and a capital under lockdown: the youth-led protests against the election chief have the attention of the Indian government. But experts say toppling…

image.caption: Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from JulyImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In its latest round of agitation, they are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide.
You can read more about the controversy here.
What happened over the weekend?
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, accompanied by co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, was detained from the plane in which he landed in the national capital on Saturday.

Meanwhile, police were stationed outside the homes of several other faces associated with the movement, including social media personality Dhruv Rathee, who has nearly 20 million followers on Instagram.

In central Delhi, buses were loaded with protesters, many of whom were taken to far-flung centers, where they were kept for hours. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city.
How the government is handling the protests
The protests come as Modi marks 25 uninterrupted years leading elected governments, first in Gujarat state as chief minister and then as prime minister of India.

Ironically, "this celebration has happened at the time when he's politically at his weakest," Delhi-based writer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told DW. Mukhopadhyay is the author of Modi's 2013 biography, "Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times."

blocks.caption: Over 30,000 security personnel were deployed ahead of the October 10 protestImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: He contrasted the government's current response with its approach in July, when thousands of young protesters took to the streets to demand the resignation of Modi's education minister over repeated exam paper leaks.
At the time, authorities had used batons, detentions and pellets to disperse the crowds gathered in central Delhi, after they had been on the streets for days.

However, this time, authorities shifted to mass security deployments and preemptive action on a large scale. This included notices to those associated with earlier protests, transport cuts, the internet cutoff and airport arrests.

blocks.caption: Thousands of protesters were detained after CJP's call for agitationImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The government has learned from its previous experience. They didn't allow people to sit at Jantar Mantar for any length of time, so it couldn't balloon," Pearl Pandya, senior analyst for Asia at global monitor ACLED, told DW.

"What's worrying is whether this becomes a playbook for the future — that you are not allowed to protest in the first place," she added, referring to the government's decision to remove the 18th-century observatory Jantar Mantar in central Delhi from the list of designated protest sites.
Authorities, however, have announced three new designated protest sites in the national capital.
Mukhopadhyay had a different reading of the situation. "The scale of this deployment is actually a defeat for Mr. Modi," he said.
Mukhopadhyay argued that it was already a setback for the government if it was forced to deploy security forces on such a scale in response to protests from a completely new socio-political movement.
Why October hasn't matched July
Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from July, with the protests against Kumar being led primarily by opposition leaders and student organizations.
Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest
"Education was far more of a cross-cutting issue... the right to vote is still seen as an intrinsically political one, where it's the opposition versus the BJP," Pandya said.
The CJP, however, has long maintained that it is non-political. This is often cited as the reason for them amassing such a large following of young followers.
Mukhopadhyay criticized that stance, saying: "You cannot raise issues about electoral neutrality... without saying that these are political issues."
Despite the differences between the previous round of CJP protests in July and the current wave of demonstrations, sociologist Surinder Singh Jodhka emphasized continuity.

"I don't think they're qualitatively different. Once again, young people are the ones who are mobilized, and they are much more encouraged because the earlier round of protests was successful," he told DW. "And it's also asking similar questions about institutions, about democracy, about transparency and accountability."
"There is a new hope for those who had earlier given up on India, and felt like the right wing was in complete control," Jodhka added.
Abrupt change of government unlikely

Dismissing comparisons with volatile protests in neighboring Nepal and Bangladesh, which brought down their governments, the analysts pointed to India's strong institutions as a safeguard against a dramatic change of government.

"India has had a very strong state system and state institutions," Jodhka explained, highlighting that even the opposition parties were asking for "the revival of institutions, rather than an overthrow of the state."
Pandya also stated that faith in the judiciary "would prevent these protests from tipping over into a popular revolution which unseats the government."
Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns
Nevertheless, she said, sustained discontent "might come to bite the government in 2029... or before that in the state elections."
It could also erode Modi's popularity, which has been a defining feature of Indian politics over the past decade, the expert indicated.
For Mukhopadhyay, the most troubling aspect of the current protests is the erosion of the electoral body's credibility.
Recalling the pride he felt when he registered to vote at 21, he drew comparisons with young Indian voters today. "The youngsters are now fighting for their vote."

articles.title: Family and sexual violence rates against Australian children rise sharply as researchers warn of ‘manosphere’
articles.summary:
Study authors say increase cannot be attributed to any one factor and list income inequality and growing awareness as other likely reasons

  • Get our

blocks.text: The sexual assault of Australian children has accelerated sharply since the pandemic, surprising researchers who expected rates to have fallen but instead found attacks on boys had risen 15.7%.
Researchers expected rates to have dropped in line with other countries around the world and warn the troubling findings show an urgent need to prevent the suffering of children.

The University of Sydney research published on Wednesday found a significant increase in violence against children between 2014 and 2024 that could be attributed to a range of factors, including income inequality and the manosphere.
An increase in reporting due to growing awareness could also partially explain the higher rate of violence, it found.

The study found a steady increase in rates of sexual assaults against girls aged up to nine (2.8% per year) and aged 10 to 17 (4.2%), with rates among boys aged 10 to 17 accelerating sharply after 2021 (15.7%).
Family violence-related assault showed a similar trend, with stable to modest increases before 2021 followed by steep increases thereafter.
Assault-related hospitalisations and child maltreatment were generally stable.
“In Australia, income inequality is at its highest point in 20 years, with substantial increases from 2021, coinciding with the acceleration of rates found in the current study,” researchers found.

“Economic stress may be especially salient in the post-2020 period, when pandemic-related financial disruptions intensified for many families, while government benefits providing economic relief, such as the JobKeeper payment scheme in Australia, ended in March 2021.

“Shifts in gender norms and online cultures may also play a role … traditional gender attitudes that favor male authority within households are resurging among young men [and] the expansion of misogynistic online communities and broader toxic masculinity narratives are associated with hostility toward women and girls.”
The research, published in the media journal JAMA Network Open, was based on an analysis of a decades-worth of Australian data from multiple sources.
These sources included national police-recorded assaults, hospitalisations, and child protection data from three Australian national agency databases.

The study’s lead author, Dr Lucy Grummitt, said researchers expected to find that the rate of violence against children had fallen, given evidence recorded in other high-income countries over the past decade regarding child protection.
That they found the opposite was impossible to attribute to any one factor, she said, but it did show the need for a less siloed approach to the issue.
after newsletter promotion

“All these different departments that are involved in the bigger picture of violence against children are just focused on one particular subset, and we don’t actually have a very clear picture of what young people are being exposed to, and how has that changed over the last decade,” Grummitt said.
“So that was kind of the rationale … I expected to see that things were kind of improving, I suppose. But that’s not really what we found.

“Violence against children is a human rights issue, it shouldn’t be falling to one government department to be monitoring this … it really is a whole-of-government issue and currently our data and our monitoring really doesn’t reflect that.”
Grummitt said that it was frustrating for researchers to discover that in some cases entire datasets they hoped to use in the triangulation were missing.
This data included one year of missing child maltreatment data for NSW and Queensland, and family violence-related assault data for Queensland, Victoria, and Western Australia also being incomplete.
The data that did exist was also not directly comparable across states, Grummitt said.
“Family domestic violence data is improving, but it’s pretty striking that in 2024 when we finished extracting the data that there weren’t already these nationally consistent definitions.”

articles.title: 2 more ex-bodyguards tell court of cash deliveries to Romualdez
articles.summary: Two more former security aides of former Congressman Zaldy Co told the Sandiganbayan about delivering suitcases filled with cash to the houses of Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez on several occasions.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 10:59pm
Two more former security aides of former Congressman Zaldy Co told the Sandiganbayan about delivering suitcases filled with cash to the houses of Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez on several occasions.
According to Maki Pulido's report on "24 Oras," Gil Navidad testified in Romualdez's bail hearing that he witnessed or personally delivered suitcases to Romualdez's various residences five times.
Romualdez’s defense team argued that Navidad had no personal knowledge of the matter, but the court dismissed most of their objections.

One of the deliveries he mentioned occurred on November 21, 2023, which was also previously cited by George Villalon and Johnny Buduan—both of whom identified themselves as former Marines and former bodyguards of Co.
According to Navidad, he knew the house in McKinley belonged to Romualdez because he used to deliver Christmas gifts there while working as a driver for a close friend of the former Speaker.
Navidad admitted that he had never seen Romualdez in person.

However, he said he knew the suitcases contained money because he had seen Co’s former staff members, John Paul Estrada and Mark Digsay, arranging the cash several times at a condo unit in BGC, Taguig.
The prosecution presented another witness, Christopher Esquivel, a former security driver for Co.
Esquibel said he knew the suitcases delivered in November 2023 contained cash because Co’s aide instructed him to be careful, explaining that they contained money to be delivered to Romualdez.
He also mentioned that Post-it notes were attached to the suitcases indicating the amount inside, which were removed before delivery.
According to Esquibel, depending on the size of the suitcase, each contained between P10 million and P17 million.
In the judicial affidavits of Navidad and Esquibel, they claimed that someone had offered them P10 million to recant their statements, though they did not reveal who made the offer.
Romualdez was not present at the continuation of his bail hearing after executing a waiver of appearance. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: BI to release Joseph Sy on SC order
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) First Division has ordered the release of nickel businessman Joseph Sy, with the Bureau of Immigration (BI) saying that it will comply.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 10:25pm
The Supreme Court (SC) First Division has ordered the release of nickel businessman Joseph Sy, with the Bureau of Immigration (BI) saying that it will comply.

In a DZBB report from Manny Vargas on Tuesday, the SC ruled in favor of Sy’s petition for habeas corpus. Suspected of being a Chinese national parading as a Filipino, Sy was arrested by Philippine authorities in 2025 when he arrived at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport from Hong Kong.
BI Commissioner Joel Viado said that the agency respected the SC’s resolution on the petition, but clarified that the Court did not settle the matter of Sy’s nationality.

“It is also noted that the case before the Supreme Court is an appeal in the Habeas Corpus Petition involving Mr. Sy, which only involves questions on legality of his detention, and not a determination on his citizenship,” Viado said in a statement.
“We are coordinating with the Department of Justice and the Office of the Solicitor General to ensure the prompt and orderly implementation of the Court's directive,” he added.
Judicial proceedings over Sy’s citizenship and identity continued. The BI exercised its mandate to investigate immigration matters, identity, and citizenship documentation.
“The legal issues arising from that investigation remain subject to judicial determination,” Viado said.
In February, the Court of Appeals ruled that the detention of the businessman was illegal.
Sy was arrested in 2025 after it was found that his biometrics matched those of a Chinese national. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Flying foxes in NSW and Victoria face mass starvation amid food shortages
articles.summary:
Rescuers respond to surge in callouts for the vulnerable bat species, which usually feeds on blossoms and tree nectar

  • Get our

blocks.text: Flying foxes are starving en masse across New South Wales and parts of Victoria, with wildlife rescuers responding to a surge in reports of “exhausted and emaciated” adults and skeletal pups.
Most reports involved grey-headed flying foxes, listed as vulnerable under federal environment laws and which usually feed on the blossoms and nectar of native trees.

They are now facing food shortages across NSW, from the northern rivers to the south coast, according to the state’s environment department. Rescue organisations in Victoria are also experiencing an uptick in callouts, particularly in East Gippsland and Castlemaine.

Rachael Smethurst, the bat coordinator at Fawna wildlife rescue on the NSW mid-north coast, said the organisation was receiving 50 to 90 calls each day – more than the total number of callouts for bats in the previous nine months.

The bats were starving, she said. “They’re coming into back yards to eat ornamental fruit trees and eating a lot of ripe and unripe cocos palms. They’re crawling around on the ground eating unripe dropped fruit, and quite literally dropping out of trees due to starvation.”
Flying foxes were staying in back yards because they lacked the energy to fly back to camp, she said. Many were already dead, including pups that had been born prematurely.
Wildlife rescue organisation Wires said the mass starvation event was likely the result of habitat loss and a dry winter, with poor seasonal flowering of eucalypts and other natives.

“Many malnourished and dehydrated female flying foxes are in the final month of their gestational period and are tragically losing their young. They just haven’t got the nutritional health or strength to produce milk or carry to full term,” the organisation said.
Some animals were displaying unusual behaviour as they struggled to find food and water. “They’re eating off the ground, drinking water from the grass after the rain, and hanging too low in trees.”

Wires wildlife vet Dr Vere Nicolson said caring for premature pups was “labour intensive and not universally successful”, with the response made more challenging due to the number of animals involved.

Tamsyn Hogarth, director of the Fly By Night Bat Clinic, said rescuers in Victoria were seeing many “exhausted and emaciated” bats and starving babies “like little skeletons”, which appeared to be coming from NSW.
after newsletter promotion

Bats spending time in people’s back yards during the day was a red flag, she said. “They’re so hungry they’re actually eating during the day, away from the safety of the camp,” she said. There were a lot of dead pups under trees, and incidents with barbed wire, dog attacks and electrocution had also increased.

“We don’t know for sure what is causing this particular incident, but food shortages can be aggravated by climatic events such as drought and El Niño conditions,” a NSW environment department spokesperson said.
The state’s health department reminded the community to avoid touching or handling bats, after 43 people were assessed having been scratched or bitten in the past two weeks.

People were encouraged to report sick or dead bats to their local wildlife rescue, Hogarth said. That enabled volunteers to check for pups, rehabilitate animals where possible, and help ease the suffering of others – although access to veterinarians able to provide euthanasia was challenging, with so many reports coming from regional or rural areas.

Hogarth said grey-headed flying foxes usually gave birth to one young per year, so the loss of so many pups would have a “terrible ripple effect” for the species. The food shortages followed thousands of heat deaths this summer, and came amid disruptions to Melbourne’s Yarra Bend camp from freeway construction works. “They’re copping it everywhere, they can’t catch a break.”

articles.title: Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing

blocks.text: Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.

The Ukrainian president described the attack on Monday as “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.

“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote on social media. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.

US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv. However, speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation was continuing and said the lack of warning over the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.

Donald Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.

He also claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me”. On Tuesday Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.

The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said. “Russia did not heed the president … The Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted.

Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.

In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. Ukraine has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.

According to the Financial Times, the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.

The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.

On Monday Russia bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.

The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House. Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.

“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine, and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.

articles.title: Conti: Drug war victims prepare mentally for ICC proceedings
articles.summary: THE HAGUE -- Victims of the war on drugs are preparing mentally and physically for proceedings before the International Criminal Court (ICC) as the case against former president Rodrigo Duterte moves…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 9:37pm

THE HAGUE — Victims of the war on drugs are preparing mentally and physically for proceedings before the International Criminal Court (ICC) as the case against former president Rodrigo Duterte moves closer to trial, a lawyer said Tuesday.

Some victims are reviewing case documents to prepare for the possibility of revisiting painful experiences, Kristina Conti, an ICC counsel representing victims, told GMA News in an interview in The Hague, where the court held its fourth status conference in Duterte’s crimes against humanity case.
“Of course, yung paghahanda sa mga gustong pumunta dito, pero may paghahanda rin silang mental. Yun yung sinasabi nilang, ‘Naku, attorney, kailangan ko na 'yan pag-isipan,’” Conti said.
(Of course, there is preparation for those who want to come here, but they also need mental preparation. They tell me, “Oh, Attorney, I need to think about this carefully.”)
Conti said some victims want to review case documents, preparing themselves as though they would have to present evidence or participate in the hearings.

The ICC case involves alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during Duterte’s tenure as Davao City mayor and Philippine president, spanning November 2011 to March 2019. Duterte denies the charges.

Tuesday’s fourth status conference was part of the proceedings leading up to the trial, with discussions focusing on preparations for the presentation of evidence and the schedule for the next stage of the case.
Hearing schedule
Conti said the schedule for the trial’s first week provides for four hours of hearings daily, divided into one-hour sessions with 30-minute breaks in between.

“Ang na-settle ay four hours everyday for the first week. One hour each, 30 minutes break in between. Magsisimula ng 10 o'clock, matatapos ng 4:30. Maganda yung hati-hati ang oras kasi makakahinga ka,” she said.

(What has been settled is four hours of hearings every day during the first week, with one-hour sessions and 30-minute breaks in between. The hearings will start at 10 a.m. and end at 4:30 p.m. It is good that the time is divided into segments because people can take a breather.)
She said the schedule was recommended by the ICC Registry, which oversees the court’s administrative and logistical arrangements, rather than by the prosecution or the victims.
Looking ahead to 2027, Conti said the defense had raised concerns about the length and intensity of the evidentiary proceedings, particularly if blocks of evidence were presented consecutively.
She said breaks of two to three weeks between evidentiary blocks could be expected, although the longer-term schedule remains subject to developments in the proceedings.
Despite questions surrounding the timetable, Conti expressed confidence that the hearings would proceed, particularly as discussions increasingly focused on evidence.
“Sa ngayon, confident ako na tuloy-tuloy ang hearing, lalo na pinag-uusapan na ang ebidensya. We're really moving forward to trial, kung saan ang pag-uusapan ay yung substantial,” she said.

(For now, I am confident that the hearings will continue, especially since the evidence is now being discussed. We are really moving forward to trial, where the substantive matters will be addressed.) —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Key organizer of Pearson gold heist says his money was taken during kidnapping in Pakistan

image.caption: Archit Grover is expected to face trial in November 2027. (Peel Regional Police)

blocks.text: Arsalan Chaudhary, who is serving four years in prison for his role in the Pearson Airport gold heist, began testifying Tuesday at the trial of former Air Canada employee Parmpal Sidhu, who is facing charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.
(Peel Regional Police)
The Latest

items: Arsalan Chaudhary, a man serving four years in prison for his role in the 2023 Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist, testified Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu. Chaudhary, who will return to the witness box Wednesday, said that the planning of the heist was "all me."

Chaudhary said he melted some of the stolen gold and received $200,000 to $300,000 for it, then travelled to Pakistan. He said he was subsequently kidnapped and abused, and when he was released the money was gone.

Sidhu is a former Air Canada employee accused of providing a doctored document that allowed for the pickup of more than $22 million in gold and currency. Sidhu pleaded not guilty earlier this month to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.
Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.
Sidhu's trial, which began in a Brampton, Ont., courtroom on Oct. 5, is before Justice Gordon Cudjoe.

blocks.text: Pinned
What we learned from Tuesday's testimony
What the 'mastermind' of the $22M Pearson gold heist had to say in court

Arsalan Chaudhary, currently serving a four-year sentence for his role in the $22-million Toronto Pearson airport heist, testified Tuesday in the trial of a former Air Canada employee. Parmpal Sidhu, the former employee, is accused of altering cargo documents to enable the massive theft of gold and cash.
It was a stuffy, packed courtroom proceeding Tuesday in the trial for Parmpal Sidhu, for his alleged involvement in the 2023 Pearson airport gold heist.

Crown prosecutors previously alleged in court that Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson cargo bay.

Arsalan Chaudhary, the 43-year-old believed to have been at the helm of the operation, testified during Sidhu's trial Tuesday. He told the Brampton Ont., court that the "planning of the gold heist was all me" and that he had "heard" of Sidhu but doesn't "really know him."

Chaudhary remained vague in his description of Sidhu, and his testimony was muddled, interrupting Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic numerous times and prompting Justice Gordon Cudjoe to tell him to "take a deep breath" before answering more questions.

Most of Chaudhary's testimony Tuesday focused on text and group chat messages related to the heist that he said he did not remember or recall. His testimony also shed light on what he did with the portion of gold that he took for himself.
According to his testimony, Chaudhary took a third of the gold from the heist and stashed it in a condo in the Greater Toronto Area. He melted it for sale, acquiring $200,000 to $300,000 in cash.
He eventually made his way to Pakistan with the money, where he said he was abducted and forced to give it up, along with the remaining gold from the condo unit in Canada.
Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.
His testimony will continue Wednesday.

articles.title: Emotions run high among Duterte supporters at ICC hearing
articles.summary: Some supporters of former president Rodrigo Duterte were teary-eyed as he waved and smiled at them before the curtains closed on the public gallery at the ICC.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 9:28pm

THE HAGUE — Some supporters of former president Rodrigo Duterte were teary-eyed as he waved and smiled at them before the curtains closed on the public gallery during the fourth status conference of his case at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Tuesday.
It was Duterte’s second physical appearance in the ICC courtroom since his arrest in March 2025. He had previously attended the September 16 status conference in person.

The public gallery was filled with Duterte supporters, representatives of human rights organizations, international media, and groups campaigning for accountability over killings during the Philippines’ war on drugs, including Duterte Panagutin Europe.

Wearing a black polo shirt, Duterte remained in the courtroom throughout the session, attentively watching the proceedings on the screens. Before the curtains closed, he waved and smiled at his supporters. Some waved back tearfully, while others continued looking through the glass separating them from the courtroom.
Among those who traveled to The Hague was Gin, a Duterte supporter who made the nine-hour journey from Germany. It was the first time she had seen Duterte in person.
“Mahal namin si Tatay Digong ko kaya andito kami. Ito lang ang pinuntahan ko dito, may trabaho ako pero special ito si Tatay Digong,” Gin said.
(We love Tatay Digong, which is why we are here. This is the only reason I came here. I have a job, but Tatay Digong is special.)

Inside the courtroom, the proceedings included a heated discussion over the prosecution’s submission of records relating to 3,400 deaths during police operations. Prosecutor Julian Nicholls cited a government report that recorded 3,967 drug personalities killed in anti-drug operations between July 2016 and November 2017. Following its review, the prosecution arrived at a figure of 3,400 deaths, which the defense disputed.

The defense questioned whether the records had been properly reviewed, while presiding Judge Joanna Korner stressed that the documents needed to be examined manually, person by person. Nicholls denied that artificial intelligence had been used to process the database, explaining that analysts had reviewed the documents under lawyers’ direction before the lawyers examined their work.

The chamber also discussed preparations for the trial, scheduled to begin on November 30. These included the time allotted for opening statements and the first block of evidence, expected in December; the prosecution’s witness list and estimated presentation time; and the time needed by the defense and the victims’ common legal representative.
Other matters included the prosecution’s evidence list, disclosure requirements, the defense’s submissions on its readiness for trial and requests for protective measures.
The conference followed an ICC ruling made public on October 8 that found Duterte fit to stand trial, clearing the way for proceedings to begin as scheduled.
Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to killings allegedly committed during his anti-drug campaign. He denies the charges. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?
articles.summary: Experts say there is no evidence that Russian trolls have been affected by Ukraine’s Yandex attacks.
articles.byline: Richard Irvine-Brown, Shayan Sardarizadeh, Adam Durbin

blocks.text: Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.

Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".
Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.
These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.
Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.
The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.

But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.
Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.

While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.

articles.title: ICC prosecutors in Duterte case to present 5 witnesses before year-end
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution team said it plans to present five witnesses in person before the tribunal before the end of the year.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 9:15pm
The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution team said it plans to present five witnesses in person before the tribunal before the end of the year.

During the ICC Trial Chamber III’s fourth status conference on Tuesday, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner sought confirmation from the prosecution on the number of witnesses expected to testify in person before the trial begins on November 30.

“They will all be present unless something unforeseen… that’s the plan; they will all be here. They will be 1302, 1100, 1400, 1263, and 0009… those are the five that we plan for this year,” ICC Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said.

The witnesses are identified by numerical codes to protect their identities. They are expected to appear before the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, and may provide testimony in person or through statements, depending on the court’s arrangements.
Nicholls said the prosecution had already dropped several witnesses for various reasons.

“We do expect that all the witnesses won’t be called, and we expect that some of the ones I won’t go into the reasons for now, but some of the witnesses we hope to call will not appear, so if we have two witnesses that give similar testimony, there’s a reason for that, which is that they both might not arrive,” Nicholls said.

Korner also questioned the prosecution’s plan to submit 1,000 newspaper clippings documenting killings in Davao City during Duterte’s tenure as mayor. Nicholls said the reports helped establish the number of killings during a period when no one was keeping track.

Korner said proceedings during the trial’s opening week, from November 30 to December 4, would be held in four daily sessions: 10 to 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., 1:30 to 2:30 p.m., and 3 to 4 p.m., following The Hague time.
The sessions will include 30-minute breaks, with a one-hour lunch break between the second and third sessions.
Duterte’s family visits
During the conference, Duterte’s defense counsel Peter Haynes proposed adjusting the trial schedule to accommodate family visits.

“Those of us who have been there know that the journey time to Davao is 30 hours. And his family, as you know, are senior politicians, congressmen, mayors, and law students, and they arrange their visits to him a long time in advance to fit their busy professional and family schedules. And you know from the medical evidence you've received how important family visits are to his mental well-being,” Haynes said.

Haynes warned that a continuous trial schedule could limit Duterte’s time with his family. He proposed having breaks in the proceedings and giving the family advance notice of the schedule so they could arrange their visits.
Korner said the court would consider the proposal.

Duterte remains detained at the ICC detention facility in The Hague. He faces crimes against humanity charges in connection with his administration’s war on drugs, which killed more than 6,000 people, according to government data. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte appears again at ICC hearing ahead of November 30 trial
articles.summary: This is the second time that the former Philippine president has personally appeared before the court since his arrest in March 2025

blocks.text: ATTENDANCE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference of his International Criminal Court case on October 13, 2026.
International Criminal Court
This is the second time that the former Philippine president has personally appeared before the court since his arrest in March 2025

items: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appeared before the International Criminal Court for a status conference ahead of his trial starting on November 30.

During the hearing, discussions focused on the prosecution's extensive evidence, including newspaper clippings, and the defense's complaints about the overwhelming amount of data provided, leading to a dispute over the use of artificial intelligence in evidence review.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte has made another appearance before the International Criminal Court (ICC) ahead of his full-blown trial slated to start on November 30.
Duterte, who’s facing three counts of crimes against humanity over his war on drugs, attended the Trial Chamber III’s fourth status conference on his case on Tuesday, October 13.

This is the second time that the former president has personally appeared before the court since his arrest in March 2025. On September 16, Duterte attended the chamber’s third status conference, marking his first personal appearance before the court.

blocks.caption: Rodrigo Duterte appears again at ICC hearing ahead of November 30 trial

blocks.text: A status conference is held by the chamber to allow parties to discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial. This is done to iron out details such as the schedule and the list of witnesses and evidence, among others.
During Tuesday’s hearing, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner disclosed the schedule of Duterte’s trial:

items: 10 am to 11 am
Lunch break: 12:30 pm to 1:30 pm
1:30 pm to 2:30 pm
3 pm to 4 pm

blocks.text: Apart from lunch, there are 30-minute breaks between sessions, given the experts’ recommendation of no sitting for more than an hour for Duterte due to his age and condition.
Recently, the Trial Chamber III ruled that Duterte is fit to stand trial. Citing experts’ analysis, Duterte was unanimously found to be in the capacity to understand:

items: instructing counsel in preparing and conducting the defense
the charges
the purpose and consequences of the proceedings
following the course of the proceedings, including the nature and implications of entering a plea
the evidence

blocks.caption: Rodrigo Duterte fit for trial, says ICC

blocks.text: Once again, the prosecution’s large number of pieces of evidence was brought up during the hearing, specifically by Presiding Judge Korner. Trial prosecutor Julian Nicholls explained that they had restructured their list based on the most important ones, including the “non-negotiables.”

Korner flagged the inclusion of newspaper clippings — called by the court as secondary sources — in the prosecution’s 5,000 documents. Nicholls explained that they included them because the clippings will provide context and corroborate the allegation of killings committed during Duterte’s mayoral reign in Davao City.

Defense lawyer Peter Haynes again complained about the prosecution’s “over 18,000” datasets, saying the material had been “literally dumped” on them. Later, Korner inquired why the defense did not take up the prosecution’s offer to review the documents and spreadsheet.
At one point, the prosecution and defense also entered into an argument after the defense accused the prosecution of using artificial intelligence (AI) in reviewing the evidence.

“But the dataset, yeah, Mr. Nicholls, I think, is saying they haven’t been read by a lawyer, and certainly I haven’t read them. You will have noticed from the filings and with the artificiality that we have to deal with this by not naming anybody, there have been three institutions that have had those documents,” said Haynes.

“One of them is an institution that is very resourceful in terms of both human resources and money, and it took a team of people from that institution one year to review the dataset. That’s how big it is. And they did it humanly. The prosecution [hasn’t] done it humanly. They’ve effectively passed it through an AI machine,” Haynes added.

“I have to object. That is completely untrue. He keeps saying that. We have gone through this dataset by analysts. We’ve gone through all of it, lawyers some of it, page by page, human, manual, 100%. Keep saying that. It’s not true,” Nicholls said in response.

blocks.caption: Rodrigo Duterte appears again at ICC hearing ahead of November 30 trial

blocks.text: The defense also had a motion, requesting that the prosecution’s evidence should be refiled and a 10,000-document limit should be imposed. Presiding Judge Korner ruled that the motion was “at the moment refused,” explaining that an arbitrary limit could cause the prosecution to violate the disclosure obligations.
Disclosure of evidence is done in the proceedings to allow the legal counsel of the accused to prepare a proper defense.

Nicholls explained during the trial that the prosecution can stipulate or agree on the fact that the drug war deaths were around 3,400. He said that this was actually lower than the number of deaths reported by the Duterte administration itself.

There were 7,884 alleged drug suspects killed, as of August 31, 2020, based on the Philippine National Police’s count. However, several human rights groups said there could be around 27,000 to 30,000 victims if vigilante killings were to be included.
Haynes argued with Nicholls about the number, saying that the figure was not all drug-related. However, the prosecution insisted that deaths were all related to Duterte’s drug war. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Indonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes 300 homes
articles.summary:
Hundreds of people displaced in Bangka Belitung province as shift in wind direction drove blaze towards settlement

An forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed…

blocks.text: A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said on Tuesday as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.

Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid, said.

“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village.
“My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.”
Another survivor, Haryanti, 50, said strong winds had fuelled the flames, which torn through homes that were made mostly of wood.
“I immediately ran to save myself. None of my belongings survived ... only the clothes on my back,” she said.
Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year.

Indonesia regularly has wildfires during the dry season, but they have been more intense this year because of the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is forecast to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land clearances that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo islands.
This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia.
Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has also grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency.
Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.
The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.

articles.title: Nord Stream: Germany puts suspected Ukrainian pipeline saboteur on trial
articles.summary: A Ukrainian citizen faces court in Hamburg, accused of attacking the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022. It raises questions about Kyiv's possible role in the explosions. German support for Ukraine is…

image.caption: Massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea after the explosion of the Nord Stream pipelinesImage: Danish Defence Command/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: The aerial photos made headlines worldwide: On September 26, 2022, massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea near the island of Bornholm. Unknown people had blown up three of the four sections of the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines from Russia to Germany.

The attack, which occurred seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, meant the end of a mega energy project between Germany and Russia in which both sides had invested billions, and which secured affordable Russian gas for Germany. However, the flow of gas via Nord Stream 1 had been restricted or stopped several times by Russia since the Ukraine war began; Nord Stream 2 was not yet operational.

From October 14, Ukrainian citizen Serhii K. is facing trial before a court in the northern German city of Hamburg. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025 on a European arrest warrant and later extradited to Germany. This week he must answer for the attacks before the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court. He is accused of being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.
5 things you need to know about Nord Stream
Ukraine aid criticized
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines.

"Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters again in August in response to a question about the ongoing investigation.

The fact that the accused is Ukrainian is especially politically sensitive. Germany continues to support the country after it was attacked by Russia: militarily, financially, with humanitarian aid and by taking in about 1.3 million refugees.

Critics of Germany's support for Ukraine, especially the right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Moscow, resume energy deliveries from Russia – including via a repaired Nord Stream pipeline — and stop supporting Ukraine. Some of them have practically delivered their verdict on Serhii K., although the trial has not yet begun, and assume that Ukraine's political or military leadership was behind the attack on the pipeline.

Sahra Wagenknecht, former leader of the BSW, told news agency Reuters in 2025 following Serhii K.'s arrest: "It is totally absurd that Germany spends many billions on aid for Ukraine but never demands an explanation from [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. Questions should also be raised about possible compensation."

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the AfD, has shared similar sentiments. In early 2026, she asserted that the German government must seek financial repayment from Ukraine. If the AfD came into power, she would demand Kyiv compensate Germany for blowing up the pipeline and pay for its repair. According to her, a country that does such things is "no friend of Germany." She has, however, failed to provide proof that Ukraine was behind the attack.
Who benefited from blowing up the pipeline?

In an interview with public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk in 2023, German naval commander Göran Swistek pointed out that, given the technical, financial, and organizational effort involved, “there is likely a state-run structure behind it.” In his opinion, a group of amateurs could not have carried out the act.

However, he considered it unlikely that this state could be Ukraine, since Ukraine, after all, would not want to jeopardize German support. At the time, Swistek thought a false lead pointing to Russia was possible.

The German-Russian Nord Stream project had many opponents from the beginning, including Poland, the US, the Baltic countries and — especially since Russia's full-scale invasion — Ukraine. That is why investigators always ask: Who benefits from the explosion?
Henning Hoff from the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) thinks it is important to shed light on the background context.

"By halting supplies or using the threat to do so as leverage, Russia exerted immense pressure on Germany at the time, and gas markets went haywire," he told DW. "The explosion thwarted Russian attempts to extort Germany, prices for natural gas sank. I think one could say: The explosion was in German interests."
Can Ukraine still count on Germany?
Berlin's dilemma

But what will happen if the Ukrainian Serhii K. is found guilty and a connection to the military or political leadership of Ukraine is proven? Could the German government still continue its current course regarding Ukraine?

The German government faces a dilemma: On one side, judicial independence must be preserved and consequences for the sabotaging German infrastructure must be pursued. On the other side, the German government wants to prevent Russia from instrumentalizing the case. However, pressure on Germany would increase enormously, also from within the country.

Roderich Kiesewetter, a lawmaker with the ruling center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), said there is no reason to deviate from the current course of support, even in the case of involvement by Kyiv: "Irrespective of the outcome, no consequences at all are appropriate, because our support for Ukraine is carried out in the interest of our own national security and stems from a sense of responsibility for a free Europe."
The debate around support for Ukraine is escalating in Germany, regardless of the court process. Public backing for Ukraine is decreasing, especially for deliveries of weapons.

The AfD gained significant support in three state parliament elections held in eastern Germany during September. The party could potentially supply the state premier in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD has also led nationwide polls for months, far ahead of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
In addition, the AfD and BSW have drawn a connection between planned government spending cuts on social services and aid to Ukraine.

Wagenknech told a campaign event before the state parliament elections that the federal government was "Sinking billions upon billions into the black hole of Ukraine, while in Germany, in our schools, the children are no longer properly learning reading, writing and arithmetic." Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of the AfD, raised the question of whether citizens were prepared to spend so much money on a non-EU and non-NATO country.
Germany's chemical industry hit by high energy prices
Repair of Nord Stream unlikely

Given very expensive energy costs, it is not only the AfD and BSW who suggest repairing Nord Stream and receiving new deliveries of gas from Russia. Some CDU politicians favor this too, such as Saxony state premier Michael Kretschmer. He views a repaired gas pipeline as a possible bargaining chip for talks with Russia. Kretschmer's position, however, contradicts the federal CDU party line and European Union sanctions policies.

His party colleague Kiesewetter considers it dangerous: "Russia has always used energy as an instrument of geo-economic extortion. It would be extremely dumb if we were to again learn nothing from history and cling to a special path with Russia. That would fuel mistrust among our partners in Europe. I can only advise everyone, including people from the CDU, to keep their distance from such calls, because they are against German interests."

Hoff from the DGAP also rejected positions like Kretschmer's. "That is an illusion. There is no returning to the time before Russia's war. The supposedly cheap Russian gas, which has cost Germany dearly, will never flow again, if only because Putin has no interest in it doing so. It serves only as an instrument of propaganda for polarizing German politics and weakening support for Ukraine."
In any case, the outcome of the trial in Hamburg will undoubtedly influence the public debate about further support for Ukraine.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Scientists call for international body to oversee advanced AI
articles.summary: In an open letter, the researchers say frontier AI models should initially be air-gapped from external networks and subject to independent oversight, arguing that voluntary industry commitments are…

blocks.text: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE. An AI sign is seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, China on July 6, 2023.
Aly Song/Reuters

In an open letter, the researchers say frontier AI models should initially be air-gapped from external networks and subject to independent oversight, arguing that voluntary industry commitments are not enough

Around 400 scientists, including AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, on Tuesday, October 13, called for an international body to oversee containment standards and incident reporting for advanced cyber-capable AI systems.
The proposed body would set industry-wide containment standards and maintain a registry of significant security incidents, which the scientists said should eventually be made public.

In an open letter, the researchers said frontier AI models should initially be air-gapped from external networks and subject to independent oversight, arguing that voluntary industry commitments are not enough.
The proposal comes a month after Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia signed a White House accord committing to voluntary safety measures without any formal enforcement mechanism.

The letter also follows a series of incidents that researchers say exposed weaknesses in how advanced AI systems are tested and contained, including cases where AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments and compromised external systems.

The signatories from 34 countries said organisations developing or testing cyber-capable models should immediately adopt high-assurance containment standards while governments work towards a more formal oversight regime.

Policymakers are increasingly debating how advanced AI systems should be supervised. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Reuters on Friday, October 9, that the bloc’s AI Act is sufficient to address risks from rogue AI systems.
On Sunday, October 11, the Trump administration lifted its block on US labs giving Britain’s AI Security Institute early access to models for safety testing.

Hinton and Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award with Meta’s Yann LeCun, another leading AI researcher. LeCun did not sign the letter and has argued that recent security incidents primarily reflect engineering failures rather than existential AI risks. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Man who witnessed deadly roller-coaster fall at Six Flags prays it was 'just a freak accident'

image.caption: Attractions are seen at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 24 kilometres northwest of Atlanta, where a man fell to his death on Tuesday. (Mike Stewart/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Interview with witness Nick Mendenhall:
As It Happens6:42Man who witnessed deadly rollercoaster fall at Six Flags prays it was 'just a freak accident'
When Nick Mendenhall decided to surprise his 14-year-old son with a trip to Six Flags, he had no idea the day would take a tragic turn.

A 42-year-old man fell to his death on Monday while riding the Goliath roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, north of Atlanta. Police say he was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride.

Six Flags has since closed Goliath and nine similar roller-coasters at six of its North American parks — including two at Canada's Wonderland north of Toronto — while investigators work to determine what went wrong. La Ronde in Montreal has also temporarily closed a roller-coaster that was acquired under the park's previous Six Flags ownership.

Mendenhall had just ridden the Goliath with his son about 15 minutes before the fatal fall, and was watching nearby when it happened. He told As It Happens guest host Dave Seglins what he saw. Here is part of their conversation.
Nick, how are you and your son holding up after what happened?

We're good. I'm still processing. There's been a lot of phone calls and messages and texts [from] people that want to talk to me about everything. And so I'm trying to process it while talking through it. I think it's in some ways, it's a healthy thing. In some ways, I think, it's little bit of a challenge. But I'm good. I am good.
And my son is doing fine.... He didn't see what I saw. He was in line for another ride when it happened. So he did not physically see it.
Can you tell us about the ride a little? Have you ridden the Goliath before?

Yes, probably 20 times in the last eight weeks. We have passes and we go often. And it's one of our favourite rides in the park. We actually had gotten off the ride about ... 10 to 15 minutes before the accident happened.
Was there anything in particular that brought you and your son to the park yesterday?
My son had asked me several times if I would take him to the park on Monday because he didn't have class. And I had told him, no, I didn't think so, I was working.
So I kind of surprised him. I started my work day a little bit early, and at about 1:30, I said, "Hey, bud, let's go to the park."

I was on phone calls and working, and he and I were just hanging, but he was fine with me working. And so when everything happened, I was on a call with a co-worker as I saw it all happen, and I said, "Hey, I gotta get off the phone. A man just fell off the roller-coaster."
Wonderland, La Ronde suspend some rides after Six Flags death
Can you tell us what you saw from your spot on the ground?
I can, and I want to try to word this in a way that's respectful and respectable.

I'm standing, I don't know, 30 or 40 feet away from the track, probably. I think I was probably 50 to 100 feet from him. I mean, I was close enough that I knew that he was a middle-aged guy. I knew it was not a kid. I knew there was only one person.

The roller-coaster car comes over a little hill that people were referring to as a bunny hop.... It's basically the last one of the ride, right before the ride ends … and I was just watching the car as it came across the track.

I saw the man come up out of his seat, I mean, almost as if you were hovering because he's moving at the same speed as the car. And his hands are kind of out in front of him. And he, almost in a diving motion, went head-first down into another car. And I was just praying, you know, "God, let this man stay in that car." I knew it was the very end of the ride and I'm thinking, "Man, if they can just hold on to him, maybe he's OK."

As the car coasted up the last little hill, it makes a hard left-hand turn into a straightaway where it breaks and then is the end of the ride. And as it made that turn, I saw him come out of the coaster altogether and fall.

At that point, I only had about a few feet of visual reference because there's a fence between where I was standing and where the track was. There's quite a bit of distance and a fence. So I saw him fall. I could not see him land or anything like that and, quite frankly, I'm glad I didn't. And more than anything, I'm glad my son was in line for another ride and didn't physically see it happen.
Just horrific.
Very, very much.
One dead, several injured after incident on a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia | Hanomansing Live
What went through your mind as you're thinking you're just watching the ride and, suddenly, this person flies out?
I think I was trying to process 150 things at one time. I don't really know what I was thinking. You know, obviously there's an instant adrenaline rush. I mean, I was shaking a little bit.

But I turned. There was a woman there that called 911, and so I didn't call 911, because sometimes the worst thing you can do is have 30 people call 911 for the same problem. There was a park employee walking up the hill. I said something to the park employee, like: "Did you see what just happened?" And they had no idea, the employee that was walking uphill. And I said: "Someone just fell out of Goliath."
I called my wife who was on her way to the park with my other three kids and herself.... I didn't want her to come to the park at that point.
I grabbed my son. He's in line. I go up to the entrance of that line and I call his name and I say, "Hey, I need you to come here a minute."
And, you know, [it's] very calm. No one's really panicking on the ground because I don't think very many people saw what happened.… I'm not sure anyone else really saw it the way that I did.
Do you have any sense of what went wrong?
None. And I don't want to speculate. So many people were posting that it was the park employees not doing their job, and they were saying just things that were just, there's no way anyone could know.

We go so often and I've never experienced a feeling of unsafe behaviour from the employees. I've never thought that they weren't doing their job. I mean, most of these are high school kids and young adults that are working their jobs for the summer and … we need to be worried about what they saw and what they experienced from a trauma perspective, not pointing fingers at them.
I hope it comes out what the cause was. And, man, I hope and pray that it was just a freak accident and it was no one's fault.

But even if it was, man, to be pointing fingers and saying things like that, that those kids will probably hop on social media and they'll see, is just, it's so sensationalist. It's so just heartbreaking.

MANILA, Philippines – Weeks after starting its investigation into Genesis88 Construction Inc., the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed complaints against its owner, Glenn Escandor, and six others, including Genesis88 employees and former officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Davao City District Engineering Office.
On Tuesday, October 13, the NBI filed falsification by public officer and graft complaints against Escandor and the following:

items: Saturnino Bentulan – authorized managing officer, Genesis88
Benjamin Zosa – project engineer, Genesis 88
Roy Bohol – construction foreman, Genesis 88
Richard Ragasa – former district engineer, DPWH Davao City District Engineering Office
Lilibeth Sarmiento – former assistant district engineer, DPWH Davao City District Engineering Office
Roberto Mamaril – former OIC-chief, Construction Section, DPWH Davao City District Engineering Office

blocks.text: The complaints came after the NBI started looking into the P1.9-billion flood control projects awarded to Genesis88, located in the district of Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte. Escandor, the Dutertes’ longtime friend, is the owner of the firm, based on Securities and Exchange Commission records obtained by Rappler in 2025.

A Rappler investigation revealed that one in four flood control projects in Davao City was awarded to Genesis88. The years when it bagged the contracts coincided with the time when Rodrigo Duterte was president and when the younger Duterte was the lawmaker representing the 1st District of Davao City.

Almost P2.9 billion (or P2,890,690,550.13) worth of contracts for flood control infrastructure from 2021 to 2023 went to the firm, based on figures from the Sumbong sa Pangulo website. This translated to a total of 35 projects — solo contracting and joint ventures with other firms included — in the region.

Escandor was former president Duterte’s assistant for sports. He also owns the Escandor Development Corporation, which donated P19.923 million for the ads of Vice President Sara Duterte during the 2022 national elections, according to the Vice President’s Statement of Contributions and Expenditures seen by Rappler. – with reports from Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

articles.title: Critics warn of espionage risks as Slovakia restores military-diplomatic representation with Russia
articles.summary: Slovakia is restoring military-diplomatic relations with Russia for the first time since 2022. The government has defended the move; critics warn of espionage risks and further damage to trust within…

image.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) welcomed Slovak President Robert Fico to the Kremlin on Victory Day in MayImage: Gavriil Grigorov/Russian Government/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: When Robert Fico sat opposite Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin in May, the Slovak prime minister said relations between their countries should extend beyond energy supplies.
He told the Russian president that steps had already been taken to restore military attaches at their respective embassies.
Five months later, the arrangement is now taking shape.

Slovakia has sent two military officers — Brigadier General Slavomir Staviarsky and his deputy, Colonel Ivo Gahir — to Moscow and is preparing to receive a Russian military attache in Bratislava, restoring military-diplomatic representation for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
What has Slovakia to gain?
The move has prompted criticism from opposition politicians, who question what Slovakia stands to gain.
They warn that Russia could use the arrangement to strengthen its intelligence operations.

blocks.caption: Fico (right, fourth from the front) told Putin (left, fourth from the front) that relations between their two countries should extend beyond energy suppliesImage: Ramil Sitdikov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "One additional military attache does not fundamentally change that broader picture; the appointment's main significance is the political signal it sends," Martin Poliacik, a former Slovak MP affiliated with the opposition Progressive Slovakia party, told DW.
"NATO allies should be concerned both about the activities of the incoming officer and about the political environment in which he will operate," he went on.
The appointments were reported by Slovak news website Aktuality.sk on October 8. Both officers appear on the Slovak Defense Ministry's published list of military diplomats serving abroad.
According to public broadcaster STVR, Staviarsky has been in Moscow since the beginning of August.
Meanwhile, opposition defense experts quoted by Aktuality.sk named the incoming Russian officer as Maxim Verezan.
Verezan has received Slovak approval, according to the opposition sources cited by the website, but was not yet listed among accredited military attaches.

blocks.caption: Brig. Gen. Slavomir Staviarsky (right, pictured here with Maj. Gen. Dale Lyles of the USA at a ceremonial delivery of fighter jets in 2024) is one of two military officers Slovakia has sent to MoscowImage: piemags/IMAGO

blocks.text: Aktuality.sk says that the Defense Ministry has not answered its question as to when Verezan is due to arrive in Bratislava.
Fear of espionage and disinformation
The prospect has revived memories of a Russian espionage scandal involving Sergei Solomasov, the Russian embassy's deputy military attache in Bratislava, a few years ago.
Solomasov was filmed recruiting and handing over money to Bohus Garbar, a contributor to the pro-Russian website Hlavne spravy in 2021.
Solomasov was expelled from Slovakia the following year. Garbar was subsequently convicted of espionage and bribery.

Opposition experts told Aktuality.sk that a Slovak attache in Moscow would be closely watched and obtain little useful information, while the reciprocal Russian posting could facilitate espionage in Slovakia.
They warned that the incoming officer could conduct influence and disinformation operations, questioning what Slovakia would receive in return.
Government defends the move
The government and its supporters have defended the renewal of contacts as a means of gathering information and maintaining diplomatic representation.

blocks.caption: General Pavel Macko, former Slovak deputy chief of defense, has called the government's decision to restore military contacts with Russia 'very serious'Image: Tutus Zmijewski/EPA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a statement reported by Slovak public broadcaster STVR, Slovak military intelligence said Staviarsky's role was to assess the security and military-political situation and keep the Defense Ministry informed.
Richard Gluck, a member of Fico's Smer party who chairs parliament's defense and security committee, pointed to the presence of American, British and French military diplomats in Moscow.
"We were losing a great deal of information," Gluck told STVR, arguing that ending Slovakia's military diplomatic presence in Moscow had been a mistake.
'A very serious step'
For retired Lieutenant General Pavel Macko, however, the circumstances in which the previous contacts ended are crucial.
"This is a very serious step taken by the Fico government," said Macko, a former Slovak deputy chief of defense and once the highest-ranking Slovak general in NATO's command structures.
"Nothing has changed [since 2022], just the opposite," he went on.

"Russia's adversarial activities continue to grow in Slovakia and in the region. The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine continues with high intensity, so do the hostile hybrid activities against Slovakia and its neighbors," Macko said.
He pointed to a foiled plot to burn down a Ukrainian-owned drone factory in eastern Slovakia and suspicions that incidents in Munich and Leipzig were linked to Russian operations based in Slovakia.

blocks.caption: Macko says that Russia's adversarial activities continue to grow in the region, pointing to suspicions that a recent incident in Leipzig was linked to Russian operations based in SlovakiaImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Macko also warned that political influence over Slovakia's intelligence services and the government's pro-Russian policies could further damage intelligence-sharing and trust among allies, despite the presence of "a significant number of very professional and trustworthy officers."
One eye on next year's election?

Martin Poliacik, meanwhile, said he suspected political motives lay behind the decision to restore the military attache posts, which comes as Prime Minister Fico eyes his chances of re-election next year.
"[Fico's] best chance of building a credible narrative for the next election is to claim that everyone else is dragging us into war and he alone wants peace," Poliacik told DW.

"I believe he will argue that he is best placed to talk to Putin about ending the war, and that this requires an exceptionally close relationship with him," he went on, adding that Fico tried to keep quiet about the major role played by Slovak arms manufacturers in supplying Ukraine with ammunition.
The ammunition is supplied under commercial contracts, rather than as military aid from the Slovak government.
Poliacik, too, distinguished between Slovakia's formal commitments and confidence in its political leadership. In his view, Western partners have become accustomed to Fico's behavior.
"Slovakia is formally fulfilling its NATO commitments," he went on.
"Formal compliance does not, by itself, settle the question of political trust," Poliacik added. "Predictability, however, is not the same as reliability."

blocks.text: A series of newly-released calls made after the failed execution of US death row inmate Christa Pike reveal emergency services were delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials.

The recordings, first obtained by the Associated Press, show that minutes passed as officials and responders attempted to confirm whether the request for emergency help in the execution chamber at Riverbend Prison was legitimate.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.
The BBC's Mayeni Jones explains.
