articles.title: How DBP botched Duterte-era contractor loans: lax checks, billions overdue
articles.summary: Meant to support the former president's Build, Build, Build drive, DBP's ICONS program instead left the bank with P4.09 billion in overdue contractor loans

items: The Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) faces over P4 billion in overdue loans from its Infrastructure Contractor Support (ICONS) program, which was intended to finance contractors for infrastructure projects under the Duterte administration.

State auditors found that DBP failed to follow proper lending safeguards, leading to significant discrepancies in loan disbursements and collections, exemplified by a P300-million loan where the contractor defaulted shortly after receiving the funds.

COA recommended investigating potential negligence among DBP staff and urged the bank to expedite recovery efforts for unpaid loans, while DBP's overall nonperforming loan ratio has increased, indicating broader financial issues.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Lapses in lending safeguards and years-long delays in collection left the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) with more than P4 billion in overdue contractor loans under a program meant to support the Duterte administration’s Build, Build, Build infrastructure drive, state auditors found.

The overdue loans amounted to 61.4% of the P6.67 billion still owed to DBP under the Infrastructure Contractor Support (ICONS) program. Launched in 2017, the program allowed contractors to borrow against expected payments from infrastructure projects, but the Commission on Audit (COA) found cases where loans were released without adequate verification of construction progress.

DBP’s board eventually approved the termination of ICONS on June 3, 2026, citing the high level of overdue loans. The closure, however, still leaves the bank with billions of pesos in debt that it may never recover.

Launched in 2017, ICONS helped finance contractors undertaking infrastructure projects under the Duterte administration’s Build, Build, Build initiative, including public-private partnership projects.

Contractors need money for construction before they receive full payment from project owners. ICONS helped bridge that gap by lending against expected contract payments, or receivables, assigned to DBP as security.

For that arrangement to work, the bank needed to verify that the projects were progressing and that the payments backing the loans could actually be collected. Under its own lending guidelines, loans were supposed to be released in stages as construction progressed, with account officers required to visit project sites before disbursing funds and continuously monitor borrowers.
But COA found that DBP’s safeguards were not always followed.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] DBP’s bad loans: The failures behind the billions

blocks.text: One P300-million loan shows how the ICONS program went wrong, from DBP’s failure to properly check the projects before releasing the money to its struggle to collect from the borrower years later.

In August 2019, DBP approved a P300-million credit line for a contractor undertaking five projects for a government-owned or -controlled corporation (GOCC). The contractor drew the full amount by March 2020, with repayment supposed to come from payments it expected to receive as construction progressed.

On paper, the projects appeared to be well underway. The two biggest projects backing the credit line – each with a contract value of more than P217 million – were reported to be 75.37% and 80.89% complete, respectively.

But DBP released the loans without actually checking how much work had actually been completed. Instead, the bank relied on the value of the contractor’s expected project payments, which covered at least 150% of the outstanding loans.

blocks.caption: OVERDUE. A comparison of the reported and actual completion rates of five projects used as security for the P300-million DBP loan, based on findings from the Commission on Audit’s 2025 report.

blocks.text: “There was no verification of the actual project accomplishment prior to loan release of the loans, as required by the Circular,” state auditors said in their 2025 report.
By June 2020, just three months after fully drawing its credit line, the contractor had already fallen behind on payments.

It was only in March 2021, a year after the full amount had been released, that DBP checked the actual construction progress with project engineers. The findings revealed substantial discrepancies between the accomplishments the contractor had reported and those subsequently verified.
Two of the projects, Projects 3 and 4, had already been ordered terminated in September 2020 due to construction delays.

“No principal repayment was collected from Borrower 1 despite repeated collection efforts and demand letters, resulting in an outstanding principal balance of P300 million as of December 31, 2025,” the COA said.

By January 2026, the situation had worsened. The GOCC confirmed to COA that four projects had been terminated, while the fifth had been fully paid in December 2021. The government company said it no longer owed the contractor anything from the five projects.

More than five years after the contractor first defaulted, DBP had yet to recover any of the P300-million principal. The bank had already set aside an allowance for the entire amount to account for the expected loss.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] DBP’s ₱36.2-B NPL exposure emerges as a state-level credit risk

blocks.text: The P300-million loan was not an isolated case.
Another contractor still owed DBP P490.46 million at the end of 2025, even though the infrastructure projects whose expected payments had been pledged to the bank as security were already completed.
COA found that the contractor had subcontracted most of the work to other companies, leaving it with a financial stake averaging just 3.5% of the projects’ contract costs.

Despite the projects being completed between 2017 and 2021, the contractor continued requesting loan extensions instead of repaying the principal. The audit did not establish what happened to the project payments or why they had not resulted in repayment to DBP.
COA also flagged significant delays in DBP’s efforts to recover overdue loans.

At DBP’s Albay lending center, a borrower defaulted in June 2021, but the first demand notice was sent only by email in July 2025, more than four years later. By the end of 2025, the borrower still owed P97.24 million of its original P100-million loan, with the bank already setting aside provisions for the possibility that the entire remaining amount would never be recovered. The account had also passed through six different officers between 2021 and 2026.

In Tacloban, foreclosure proceedings had yet to begin on a P82.21-million loan that had been overdue since September 2021 because the lending center lacked a full-time lawyer. Its cases were instead being handled by DBP’s Zamboanga legal team.

COA recommended investigating possible negligence among bank officers and employees handling ICONS loans, with administrative or legal cases to follow where warranted. It also urged DBP to act faster in recovering unpaid loans, particularly from borrowers still in operation or those with real estate pledged as collateral.
DBP told auditors that its management committee had directed its Legal Services Group to “investigate possible negligence in the credit administration of the loan accounts mentioned.”
But DBP had been looking into some of its largest bad loans for years before it decided to shut down ICONS.

As early as January 19, 2022, the bank’s board had ordered an inquiry into its 20 largest nonperforming loans, including the P300-million ICONS account. Yet it was only on June 3, 2026 – more than four years later – that DBP’s board approved the termination of ICONS.

Meanwhile, DBP’s loan problems extend beyond ICONS. Its gross nonperforming loan (NPL) ratio, which measures the share of loans classified as nonperforming, rose from 7.05% in December 2025 to 9.52% in March 2026, before easing slightly to 9.17% in June, according to data published by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.
These figures cover DBP’s entire loan portfolio, and it is unclear how much ICONS contributed to the deterioration of the bank’s NPL ratio.

Rappler sought DBP’s comment on how much of the P4.09 billion in overdue ICONS loans it has recovered as of present, what is driving its elevated NPL ratio, and what became of the 2022 inquiry, including why the program was terminated only in 2026.

The bank has yet to formally respond as of press time, although a representative told Rappler that it stood by the explanations it had submitted to COA. This story will be updated if the DBP responds. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Houthis and Saudis strike each other in latest escalation
articles.summary: Fighting has continued between Iran-backed rebels and Saudi Arabia, adversely impacting the kingdom's economy and security. Still, Saudi officials have stopped warning of Houthi attacks in an effort…

image.caption: Beyond attacking the capital Riyadh, Iran-backed Houthi rebels have gone after Saudi oil and transport infrastructureImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Tuesday said that Saudi Arabia had carried out overnight airstrikes targeting border regions in Yemen.
Rebel-run satellite television said two strikes had hit the Red Sea island of Kamaran and a third targeted Qanawis, north of Hodeida port.
Further strikes were reported in Jawf and rebels said their forces had downed a Saudi drone over Saada, a Houthi stronghold.

The strikes came just hours after air-raid sirens blared and loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which has come under intense fire for the past several days as fighting between the two belligerents intensifies.
The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.

The rebels have pounded Saudi Arabia in recent days, repeatedly attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On Saturday, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.

On Tuesday, Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for an immediate end to Houthi attacks on the kingdom, telling Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi that there is "no justification for these attacks and they cannot be accepted."
Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis
Houthi attacks' economic impact on Saudi Arabia
Beyond reigniting fighting tied to Yemen's civil war, increased Houthi activity has come as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on February 28.
A regional proxy, the Houthis have helped Iran further destabilize the region by striking largely at the oil and transport infrastructure that brings oil and gas from US allies in the gulf to market.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter and Houthi attacks have not only raised security issues, they have greatly hampered the kingdom's ability to get its product to market.

In its latest annual World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Saudi GDP will contract by 3.3% on the year as a result, with Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz compounded by Houthi maneuvering in the Red Sea and attacks on Saudi oil refineries and tankers.

Saudi Arabia quickly diverted oil exports away from Hormuz as Iran's blockade dragged on, making use instead, of its overland pipelines and Red Sea access. Houthi attacks, however, have also dramatically impacted these.
Houthi attacks on Saudi airports raise stakes for Washington
Saudi Arabia stops issuing air raids
The devastation of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to seek help from Washington and US President Donald Trump.
Although he previously ignored Saudi requests for assistance, on Saturday Trump mused about joining the fight against the rebels.
News of this consideration drew a quick response from the Houthis, with a representative saying US interests in the region would be targeted should DC enter the fray.
Despite at least 18 people being killed and more than 300 injured in recent days, Saudi Arabia has stopped issuing air raid alerts in the kingdom.
The government has not spoken of the policy change but observers suggest it may be an effort to avoid stirring public panic as the country's security vulnerabilities come into focus.
Still, analysts warn that the change could have the opposite effect by amplifying uncertainty over the current situation.
Last week, prior to a string of airport attacks, government officials said the alerts had been halted due to citizens' complaints about being woken by them.

Further, Saudi government officials on Monday reminded residents of regulations issued in March that forbid sharing any images related to Houthi air attacks, including missile interceptions or impact craters.

Former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney told Reuters news agency that Riyadh — which initiated public warnings in May before halting them on September 29 — was trying to balance public messaging with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but that in his opinion leaders had ended up adding to a sense of unease about Houthi airstrikes.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?

articles.title: SWS: More Filipino families rate themselves 'poor' at 55%, highest in Mindanao
articles.summary: Fifty-five percent of Filipino families rated themselves as “poor” in a survey conducted in September 2026, with the highest prevalence recorded in Mindanao, the Social Weather Stations (SWS) said…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 7:51pm

Fifty-five percent of Filipino families rated themselves as “poor” in a survey conducted in September 2026, with the highest prevalence recorded in Mindanao, the Social Weather Stations (SWS) said Tuesday.

In a self-rated poverty (SRP) survey conducted from September 21 to 27, 2026, respondents evaluated their household's poverty status and specified the minimum monthly home budget required to avoid being considered poor.
The percentage of self-rated poor families represents a six-point increase from 49% in June 2026, which SWS estimates is equivalent to approximately 16.8 million families.
Self-rated poverty was highest in Mindanao (64%), followed by the Visayas (63%), Balance Luzon (51%), and Metro Manila (44%).

“The 6-point rise in the nationwide Self-Rated Poverty score between June 2026 and September 2026 was led by a 10-point increase in Balance Luzon, combined with smaller increases in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao,” the survey firm explained.
Meanwhile, the percentage of families categorizing themselves as “borderline” dropped from 14 percent in June 2026 to 9 percent in September 2026.
The percentage hardly changed for “not poor” families at 36 percent, down just one point from 37 percent in June 2026.
Food poverty
Survey participants were also asked to evaluate their food poverty status based on the type of food their families consumed.
In September 2026, the survey found that Self-Rated Food Poverty (SRFP) rose by eight percentage points, from 36 percent in June 2026 to 44 percent.
This translates to an estimated 12.2 million self-rated food-poor families.
Meanwhile, families rating themselves as not food-poor fell from 49 percent to 47 percent, while those in the borderline category dropped from 15 percent to nine percent.
“The September 2026 SRFP rate of 44% was 3 points above the 41% annual average of 2025, and the highest since the 51% in December 2024,” SWS noted.
Poverty Threshold
The September 2026 survey also asked self-rated poor respondents for the minimum monthly income their households need to no longer be considered poor.
Based on the participants’ responses, the national median SRP threshold rose to P15,000, up from P14,000 in June 2026.
Additionally, the SRP Gap, or the self-reported shortfall in monthly household income, increased from P5,000 to P6,000.

The SWS survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,500 adults (18 years old and above) nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages, ±4% for Balance Luzon, and ±6% each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: ICC prosecution, Duterte defense clash over drug war deaths dataset
articles.summary: The prosecution team of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and lawyers for former president Rodrigo Duterte clashed over a dataset on drug war fatalities on Tuesday.

blocks.text: The prosecution team of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and lawyers for former president Rodrigo Duterte clashed over a dataset on drug war fatalities on Tuesday.
During the ICC Trial Chamber III’s fourth status conference, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked whether the prosecution had reviewed each document for its relevance to the case.

“We have got to try to sort this out. First thing, I need to know, Mr. Nicholls, from you, because it’s not clear from what you say, has the prosecution actually reviewed the database for the relevance of each individual item?” Korner said.

ICC prosecutor Julian Nicholls said the prosecution had reviewed the documents with the help of experts. Based on official Philippine National Police (PNP) records, they had identified more than 3,400 drug war deaths from July 2, 2016, to November 27, 2017.

“The analytical memo, which we have disclosed… they have counted these. These are official PNP documents, turned over… official PNP documents. I’ll leave it at that. And they have counted up to 3,422 deaths. Our proposed agreed facts are that the number is 3,400 deaths,” Nicholls said.
Nicholls added that the findings were also supported by a report from the Presidential Communications Operations Office, now known as the Presidential Communications Office.
However, he said the prosecution and the defense had yet to reach an agreement, despite the prosecution’s invitation for Duterte’s team to review the cases with them individually.
Korner noted that the documents had apparently not been reviewed individually by lawyers, stressing that the process had to be undertaken despite the resources it would require.
“I know it uses a lot of manpower, but it is something you have to do,” she said.

Duterte’s defense counsel, Peter Haynes, meanwhile, argued that the prosecution should refile the documents, raising concerns about the alleged use of artificial intelligence (AI) in reviewing the dataset.
“The Prosecution hasn't done it humanly; they effectively passed it through AI,” Haynes said.
Nicholls disputed the allegation, maintaining that the data had been reviewed entirely by humans.
In an interview in The Hague, Kristina Conti, an ICC counsel representing victims of the war on drugs, said the dispute over the number of deaths could become a major obstacle in the proceedings.

“Sa ngayon may 57 incidents na pag-uusapan dito, pero labas dito ay may 3,400 killings na gustong ipa-stipulate ng prosecution at mukhang dito tayo sasabit dahil maraming usapin kung ganon kalaking numbers na DIPO (deaths in police operations),” Conti said.

(At present, there are 57 incidents to be discussed here, but outside these are 3,400 killings that the prosecution wants to have stipulated. This appears to be where we could encounter difficulties because there are many questions when dealing with numbers as large as these involving deaths in police operations.”)
Conti said the prosecution and defense needed to resume discussions to resolve their differences over the documents.

“Yung major contention ay yung pag-admit sa bilang killings mula July hanggang November 2017. Sabi ng prosecution, may document for 3,400. Sabi ng defense, ‘Yung inyong database nyo, di nyo naman binasa nang maayos, kaya di namin at all sisilipin yan,’” she said.

(The major point of contention is the admission of the number of killings from July to November 2017. The prosecution says it has documentation for the 3,400 killings. The defense says, ‘You did not properly examine your own database, so we will not even look at it.’)
While acknowledging that both sides had arguments to make, Conti criticized what she viewed as the defense’s lack of cooperation with the prosecution.
“Kailangan sila mag-usap ulit. Medyo nagmamatigas ang defense kasi kailangan nila lumambot kasi di yan magmomove forward,” she said.
(They need to talk again. The defense is being somewhat stubborn, and they need to soften their position because this will not move forward otherwise.)
Conti also questioned the time the defense reportedly expected to need to process the documents, saying the review should not necessarily take a year given the resources available to the parties.
“Hindi ko makita yung point na one year daw ipaprocess. Ngayong hawak mo na yung document, baka naman di aabot ng one year with the resources that they have,” she said.

(I do not see the point of saying that it would take a year to process. Now that they have the documents, perhaps it will not take a year, given the resources they have.) —with Sophia Balod-Lorenzo in The Hague/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Pope Leo's surgery to remove lung nodule completed 'successfully': Vatican
articles.summary: The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a week-long hospital stay, and the Vatican has cancelled all Pope Leo's audiences through Oct. 20.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV leaves the Vatican on Tuesday for the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome, where he was operated on to remove a lung nodule. (Andrew Medichini/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a week-long hospital stay, and the Vatican has cancelled all Pope Leo's audiences through Oct. 20.
Pontiff, 71, is expected to stay in hospital for a week
Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery Tuesday to remove a lung nodule and the Vatican said the operation was completed "successfully, on schedule and as planned."
The 71-year-old Leo returned to his room after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, according to a statement from the Vatican spokesman, who promised further information at a later time.

Leo had walked into the hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening.

"Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here," said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
People wait for Pope Leo to arrive at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome ahead of his operation. (Alessandra Tarantino/The Associated Press)

The 71-year-old American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20.

"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation," said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology (EIO) in Milan, who is not involved in the pope's care but knows the team at Gemelli.

A churchman who saw Leo on Monday, Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, said Leo told him he felt fine and decided to have the surgery immediately so that he wouldn't have to alter his upcoming travel plans to Latin America.

But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
'A bit of luck'

Leo, elected ‌by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had health issues previously.

A nodule ⁠on the lung is a small, localized lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than five per cent of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although ‌risk rises with age, size and other factors, such as smoking.

items: Pope Leo will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung

blocks.text: Dr. Federico Venuto, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome's Policlinico Umberto I hospital, said procedures to remove lung nodules are usually minimally invasive, and can sometimes involve ​use of a thin camera tube called a thoracoscope.
"The complication rate is extremely low," he ⁠said.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said. Spaggiari, at EIO in Milan, said the pope has likely undergone other tests before being recommended for surgery.
"I think he has had a bit of luck. They found something that was asymptomatic — a lung nodule, possibly a tumour. He might call it something else; we call it luck," he said.
The pontiff is expected to spend a week in hospital after the operation. (Gregorio Borgia/The Associated Press)
November trip to South America

EIO advises patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery, which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery.

The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometres on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"I think the Holy Father is in excellent hands at Gemelli," Spaggiari said. "They have everything needed to keep the Holy Father alive for a long time."
Pope Leo urges compassion for migrants during Spain trip
Kikuchi, the Tokyo archbishop who is also head of the Vatican's charitable federation Caritas Internationalis, said Leo told him he felt no different than usual and was looking ahead to the trip.

"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency," Kikuchi wrote on the Facebook page of the Tokyo archdiocese.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Nuremberg airport briefly closed after in-flight emergency
articles.summary: Police are investigating a suspected in-flight emergency on a Corfu flight. After the airport reopened, the airline said they believed the emergency code was a result of a technical malfunction.

image.caption: Special police units at Nuremberg airport after an alert aboard a passenger plane prompted a temporary closureImage: Tizian Gerbing/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police gave the all-clear at Germany's Nuremberg airport after a suspected in-flight emergency involving a plane arriving from the Greek island of Corfu.
The alert prompted police to cordon off the airport and Eurofighter jets to escort the aircraft, which landed safely, an airport spokesman said.
Authorities confirmed later on Tuesday that the airport had resumed normal operations.
Coredon Airlines, which was operating the flight in question, said they believed an emergency signal had been sent due to a technical malfunction.
Why was the airport closed?
The DPA news agency reported that the plane had transmitted an emergency code before landing, alerting air traffic control to a possible problem on board.
"Checks at the scene established that there is no danger," police said in a statement. The nature of the alert was not immediately clear.
Earlier in the morning, three pilots independently reported seeing an object that may have been a drone while taking off or landing at the airport.

blocks.caption: An onboard alert on a Corendon flight from Corfu prompted a temporary closure of Nuremberg airportImage: Daniel Löb/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Airport officials, border police and Germany's air traffic control service immediately launched a search involving a police helicopter, but no drone was found.
Six flights were delayed, while two arriving aircraft diverted to Cologne and Prague before continuing to Nuremberg. It was initially unclear whether the two incidents were connected.
It was initially unclear whether the incidents were connected.
Drone incidents disrupt German airports
German airports have faced drone-related security alerts previously. In August, an explosives-laden drone was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, prompting a police investigation.
Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany
In May, a possible drone sighting halted flights at Munich airport for about an hour, forcing more than 20 arriving aircraft to divert. Police found no drone.

articles.title: Quezon City government dissolves Task Force Disiplina after officer kills 3 teenagers
articles.summary: Created in 2019 through an executive order, Task Force Disiplina was mandated to enforce city ordinances, rules, and regulations

blocks.text: TASK FORCE. Members of the Quezon City Task Force Disiplina attends a flag ceremony on October 12, 2026.
Quezon City Task Force Disiplina/Facebook
Created in 2019 through an executive order, Task Force Disiplina was mandated to enforce city ordinances, rules, and regulations

MANILA, Philippines – The Quezon City government abolished its Task Force Disiplina (Discipline) on Tuesday, October 13, following the killing of three teenagers by one of its members in Barangay Batasan Hills.

Task force member Alvince Tolentino, who was reportedly drunk at the time, shot the three teenagers on Monday, October 12, The Philippine Star reported. Batasan Police Station commander Gemmer Tubiera said the officer confronted the teenagers, who were still outside during curfew hours. The shooting happened at 2 am along Senatorial Street corner Batasan-San Mateo Road, Barangay Batasan Hills, according to the Quezon City Police District. One of the fatalities was a minor.
The suspect is now in police custody and faces three counts of murder.
Created in 2019 through an executive order, Task Force Disiplina was mandated to enforce city ordinances, rules, and regulations.
The Quezon City government clarified that it had not issued firearms to members of the task force.
Following the abolition, Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte ordered task force members to return to their mother unit, the Department of Public Order and Safety (DPOS).

Belmonte also required the members to undergo background checks, neuropsychological examinations, and drug tests, as well as submit clearances from the National Bureau of Investigation and the police, to retain their posts at the DPOS.

“Walang buhay na dapat mawala dahil sa iresponsableng paggamit ng armas. Kaligtasan ng mamamayan ang pangunahing tungkulin ng lokal na pamahalaan, at walang puwang sa serbisyo publiko ang sinumang hindi makakasunod dito,” the Quezon City government said in a statement.

(No life should be lost because of the irresponsible use of firearms. The safety of the public is the primary responsibility of the local government, and there is no place in public service for anyone who cannot uphold this duty.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Four years on, Marcos’ door for comms chiefs still revolving
articles.summary: Is sixth time the charm for President Marcos in this rather volatile Cabinet post?

blocks.text: LINO CAYETANO. TV director and producer Lino Cayetano during the 2025 election campaign. He ran for Taguig 1st District congressman.
Lino Cayetano's Facebook page
Is sixth time the charm for President Marcos in this rather volatile Cabinet post?

Just over a year after announcing a new communications secretary, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. found himself in familiar territory: having to explain the appointment of yet another chief of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO).

Is the sixth time the charm? Lino Cayetano, former Taguig City mayor and PTV-4 general manager, will be taking on a post that’s been occupied by five different people in the past four years of Marcos.

Here’s how Marcos framed Dave Gomez’s exit and Cayetano’s entry in an interview with media on Tuesday, October 13: “The reason that we keep turning, we have this high turnover is because the job keeps changing in terms of what we are trying to put forward.”

Marcos added: “In the beginning, we were talking about policy and now we are talking about — then we started talking about what we had to do in terms of implementation. And then we started having to talk — now we are having to talk about getting more towards the more political aspects of the communications job.”

“So, it keeps changing and that’s why we have to keep restructuring it and to be able to satisfy what… especially the demands that you make upon our Presidential Communications group. So yes, that’s what’s behind that.”
Let’s take a small step back and drill down on a line the President uttered: “Now we are having to talk about getting more towards the more political aspects of the communications job.”
Political? If we’re referring to political pedigree and experience, then new Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano would certainly have much to boast of.

Cayetano is the youngest in the current generation of his clan in politics. He also happens to be estranged from his older siblings, Pia and Alan Peter, who are both senators. All three (plus another sibling) are the children of the late former senator Rene Cayetano.

The youngest of the Cayetano clan in politics has held various posts in government — from barangay (village) chief, to district representative, to mayor. He tried to return to Congress in the 2025 polls but lost to a candidate who was backed by his sister-in-law Lani, Senator Alan Peter’s wife.
The older Cayetanos belong to the minority in the Senate that’s identified with Vice President Sara Duterte, Marcos’ erstwhile ally.
Lino Cayetano was also a film and TV director before joining politics full-time.
But what political aspect of the communications job must the new PCO chief pay attention to?

With just under two years left in the administration, two things would probably be foremost in the minds of Malacañang and the new communications chief: the Marcos administration’s legacy and, in relation to that, setting a favorable environment ahead of the 2028 presidential elections.

Cayetano would be the first communications chief under Marcos to have held an elected position in the past. The first communications secretary under Marcos was vlogger Trixie Cruz-Angeles, who was eased out in the first three months of the Marcos administration.
She was followed by Cheloy Garafil, who chaired the Manila Economic and Cultural Office (MECO) before being appointed secretary general of the House of Representatives.

Cesar Chavez, a radio broadcaster and long-time political communications operative, held the post for just over six months. Before Gomez, former ABS-CBN journalist Jay Ruiz was the administration’s primary communications person for four months.

Gomez, who once worked at Philip Morris International Philippines, at least held on to the position for over a year — despite never having faced the Commission on Appointments (CA). That he was bypassed by the CA is part of why he had to be replaced. Talk, for a while, has been that he would have had a hard time hurdling the CA anyway, precisely because of his previous role in a tobacco giant company.

Will Lino Cayetano at least get close to the length of Garafil’s term (almost two years) — which is to say, will he stay on until the end of this administration? If the President’s statements are any indication, that’ll all depend on the “demands that you make upon our Presidential Communications group.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Prosecution: No denial of due process over withdrawal of three charges vs. Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said Vice President Sara Duterte was not being denied due process amid its withdrawal of three of the four Articles of Impeachment against her, saying her…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 7:25pm

The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said Vice President Sara Duterte was not being denied due process amid its withdrawal of three of the four Articles of Impeachment against her, saying her defense lawyers were given ample time to question witnesses.

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas and private prosecutors Lorna Kapunan and Amando Ligutan made the position amid the defense's staunch opposition to the prosecution's bid to drop the three articles, a pleading granted by the Senate impeachment court.

The prosecution decided to drop Article I on confidential fund misuse, Article III on bribery, and Article IV on assassination plot, grave threats, and inciting to sedition against the President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. and his family.

This was after a week of testimonies from the Anti-Money Laundering Council, bank and insurance firm officials, the Bureau of Internal Revenue, as well as financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, who were called upon by the prosecution to shed light on the alleged unexplained wealth of the vice president and her husband, lawyer Manases "Mans" Carpio.

Article II remains pending before the Senate impeachment court, relating to the couple's alleged unexplained wealth, including their undeclared assets and non-divestment of business interest amid a constitutional prohibition.

"I do not really understand why they are raising the issue on fairness and injustice when in fact the effect of withdrawal is even the evidence presented by the prosecution on withdrawn articles will no longer be considered by the impeachment court. The defense is under no obligation to present their evidence [on these withdrawn charges]. What is the reason for you to present evidence to answer the allegation when in fact it doesn't exist anymore because the same have been withdrawn already by the prosecution," Luistro said in a press conference.

"And let us remember that during the direct examination by the prosecution, they were given super ample time to conduct their cross [examination]. As a matter of fact, ang dami niyang ipinilabas na mga documents through the big screen na nakita rin ng sambayanang Pilipino. If their purpose is for their evidence to be seen by the public, they have a lot of platforms to do that as has been done regularly by the respondent herself," Luistro added.
Kapunan agreed, saying the vice president should stop playing the victim.

"They always play the victim card. Pagod na po tayo sa sinasabi nilang we are the victims. Wait a minute. Hindi siya ang victim, ang taong bayan ang victim dito (We are so tired of them saying they are the victims. Wait a minute. She is not the victim. It is the public who is the victim here). You're talking about public funds, you're talking about a public officer and the impeachment, an accountability mechanism," Kapunan said.

"They keep on saying she is being persecuted. That is not correct. Who is being unfair here? Who is being unjust? The vice president herself. She refuses to come and defend herself in the impeachment court. And yet she does press conferences saying this trial is a farce. And because she is in a press conference, it was not under oath, she cannot be cross examined and asked clarificatory questions. If that is their style, then they come to court with unclean hands," Kapunan added.
Ligutan also said the defense crying injustice is totally misplaced.

"The term that they used is they were not given opportunity to test the evidence of the prosecution. I beg to disagree. That is totally wrong. They were given the opportunity to cross-examine [witnesses] and present videos, photos, statements, news articles," Ligutan said.

"They cannot say they were deprived of presenting countervailing facts. They cross-examined all our witnesses for hours, for days. The defense cannot say they were not given a fair shake," Ligutan added.
Ultimately, Ligutan said any seasoned trial lawyer knows that withdrawal of charges is a fair game in criminal procedure and thus, the defense team should have been prepared for such.

"If you are into litigation, you should prepare for all contingencies. The dropping of some articles [or cases]… that is a usual occurrence in our courts. The defense should have been more flexible," Ligutan said.
"Saan ka makakakita ng defense team na ayaw 'yung pangyayari na 'yung prosecution is withdrawing charges and banking on one solid Article of Impeachment?" Ligutan said.
(Where do you see a defense team opposing the withdrawing of charges against their client and one solid Article of Impeachment?)
Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison on Tuesday said that after 38 days of trial, the prosecution already spent considerable time and government resources presenting evidence and witnesses.
As such, Sison argued, the public has already been exposed to allegations relating to the three dropped articles while the vice president has yet to refute these.
She maintained, however, that the prosecution's move would not affect the defense panel's presentation of its own evidence. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia visit Ceuta
articles.summary: The royal couple have arrived for their first-ever visit to the exclave to show solidarity with residents.

image.caption: Felipe is the first Spanish monarch to visit the city in nearly twenty yearsImage: Pedro Nunes/REUTERS

blocks.text: King Felipe VI and his wife Queen Letizia arrived in Ceuta on Tuesday afternoon to talk to local leaders and meet with residents still dealing with a major incident at the border with Morocco over the summer.
The trip marks the first royal visit to Ceuta, and Spain's other exclave in the area Melilla, since Felipe's father Juan Carlos I toured the cities in 2007.
Excited crowds gathered to welcome the royals, with some noting that it felt like national authorities were finally paying attention to their plight.
What happened in Ceuta?
In late July, some 80,000 refugees in Morocco rushed the border fence with Spain. More than 140 people were killed in the scuffle.

The incident threw the city of some 84,000 residents into the international spotlight, with calls from right-wing governments within the European Union to suspend the Schengen free movement agreement with Spain.
How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance

However, it soon became clear that most of the refugees were quickly turned back to Morocco, and because of Ceuta's remote location, none moved on to mainland Europe except a group of at-risk children.

At the same time, locals complained that national officials did little to help with at least 10,000 migrants still in the city, and the alleged human traffickers trying to capitalize on the situation.
Meanwhile, the migrants who have been unable to return to Morocco have accused Spanish police of brutality and other abuses.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has accused organized groups stemming from Russia and Israel for spreading misinformation regarding alleged changes in Spain's immigration rules.

The incident also exposed diplomatic tensions between Spain and Morocco. Morocco does not recognize Madrid's claim to Ceuta, which has been under Spanish control for centuries. It remains to be seen how Rabat will react to Felipe's trip.

articles.title: Formula 1: Rwanda to bring sport back to Africa
articles.summary: The last time Formula 1 hosted a race in Africa was way back in 1993. But a new track in Rwanda is set to host a Grand Prix in "the early 2030s" continuing the country’s investment in international…

image.caption: Rwanda's President Paul Kagame has invested plenty in sports, with F1 a major coupImage: Bright Emoja/AFP

blocks.text: After nearly 40 years of false starts, motor racing's premier sport is returning to Africa, after Formula 1 announced on Tuesday that Rwanda would soon host a Grand Prix.

The race will be know as the African Grand Prix after a 10-year contract was signed between the parties. With no suitable track ready, Rwanda will build one in Bugesera, southeast of the capital Kigali. F1 said it will be ready "early in the next decade."

The last time F1 raced in Africa was the South African Grand Prix in 1993. While there has since been plenty of talk of the sport returning to the continent, most often South Africa itself, nothing concrete had happened, until now.
A race in every continent

"Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1," F1 President and chief executive Stefano Domenicali said. "With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."

One of the most vocal proponents of a race in Africa has been seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton. The 41-year-old Black British driver, currently with Ferrari, has said he has been "fighting in the background" for years to have a race in Africa. With the date not yet set in stone for the African Grand Prix, it remains to be seen whether he can prolong his career enough to be on the grid when the lights go out in Rwanda.
Kagame all in on sports but sportswashing claims loom

For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the event is "a success and a milestone for the entire continent, especially for the African fans." He added that he hoped it could lead to more F1 events in Africa.

Kagame has been president of Rwanda for 25 years and essentially ran the country for the six years before that after the genocide in 1994. He routinely wins over 99% of the vote in elections in a country often criticized for its human rights record.

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich ended a commercial deal with 'Visit Rwanda' last yearImage: Bernd Feil/M.i.S./IMAGO

blocks.text: The 68-year-old has bet big on sports. Rwanda has had sponsorship deals with a number of top European football clubs, including Arsenal, Atletico Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich. However, fan and media backlash over the deal caused Bayern to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year. Arsenal did not renew its deal. Many critics have labeled the policy as sportswashing.
The country also has deals with top US basketball and American Football teams, and hosted cycling's Road World Championships last year.
But Formula 1, one of the world's richest sports, will likely be seen as Kagame and Rwanda's biggest sporting coup to date.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What 'piercing the corporate veil' means
articles.summary: The doctrine of piercing the corporate veil has been raised during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, as defense and prosecution lawyers debated the assets and earnings of…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 7:16pm

The doctrine of piercing the corporate veil has been raised during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, as defense and prosecution lawyers debated the assets and earnings of companies linked to Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

The issue arose after Atty. Alexander Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst presented as a prosecution witness, testified that Duterte and Carpio supposedly had unexplained wealth and undeclared assets amounting to P817.87 million.

Cabrera said he arrived at the figure by piercing the corporate veil, a legal doctrine that allows courts, under certain circumstances, to disregard a corporation’s separate legal personality and hold the individuals behind it accountable.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison later challenged Cabrera’s testimony, describing his conclusions as “unbridled and erroneous conclusions of law and fact.”

She cited the Supreme Court’s ruling in Kukan International Corporation v. Reyes, which states that "wrongdoing must be established clearly and convincingly before a corporation’s separate juridical personality can be disregarded," and that such wrongdoing "cannot be presumed."
“Otherwise an injustice that was never intended may result from an erroneous application. And it bears reiterating that piercing the veil of corporate fiction is frowned upon,” Sison said.
When can the corporate veil be pierced?

In its ruling, the Supreme Court said the doctrine may be applied when a corporation’s separate legal personality is used to “defeat public convenience, justify wrong, protect fraud, or defend crime, or when it serves as a shield to confuse legitimate issues."

The doctrine may also apply when a corporation is "merely the alter ego or business conduit of an individual, or when its organization, control and operations effectively make it an instrumentality, agency or extension of another person or corporation."

The High Court also explained that while a corporation may be established for any lawful purpose, courts may treat it as "an association of persons or merge two corporations into one when their separate legal identities are used to conceal fraud or illegality."
In such cases, the corporate structure cannot be used to shield those responsible from liability.
Sison said she cited the ruling to "avoid misleading the public" watching the impeachment proceedings.

She questioned the basis of Cabrera’s conclusions, saying the witness had repeatedly acknowledged that he had insufficient time to conduct his analysis and did not have all the documents needed to form a sufficient basis for a complete opinion.

“Now that witness has answered over time and repeatedly that unang una sa lahat, wala siyang sapat na oras. Pangalawa, hindi niya hawak ang lahat ng dokumento to form sufficient basis or ng kumpletong opinyon,” Sison said.

(That witness has repeatedly answered that, first and foremost, he did not have sufficient time. Second, he did not have all the documents needed to establish a sufficient basis for a complete opinion.)
Diokno moved to strike Sison’s characterization of Cabrera’s testimony as “erroneous,” arguing that it was a legal conclusion and was “totally out of order.”

“It’s up to the Honorable Court to decide whether the opinion of Atty. Cabrera is acceptable or not. And it’s not in our place, whether I’m for the prosecution or for the defense, to make such irresponsible statements. I move to strike, Your Honor,” Diokno said.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, however, ruled that Sison’s remarks would remain on the record.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Climate change poses a challenge to earthquake, tsunami preparedness -- OCD
articles.summary: Climate change has made it more challenging for agencies and stakeholders to prepare for earthquakes and tsunamis as it leaves them with less time to respond to potential disasters, the Office of…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 7:02pm

Climate change has made it more challenging for agencies and stakeholders to prepare for earthquakes and tsunamis as it leaves them with less time to respond to potential disasters, the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said Tuesday.

During the World Tsunami Awarness Day press conference in Quezon City, OCD-NCR director George Keyser said the return period of major natural events has become shorter and more intense over time due to climate change.
These natural events include storms and earthquakes.
"Malaki talaga ang epekto ng climate change (sa disaster preparedness)," Keyser said. "Paikli ng paikli yung return period."
(Climate change has greatly affected disaster preparedness. the return period of natural events has become shorter.)
This led agencies like OCD to conduct several meetings with stakeholders in order revise intial preparedness and response plans.
Aside from climate change, Keyser said the lax perception of the public about disasters is also a challenge when it come to preparedness.
"Yung number one challenge talaga ito, yung perception na baka hindi man mangyari yan. Yung mabala na, yung ayaw mag-prepare," the OCD official said.
(The number one challenge is the perception of the public about disasters that it may not happen. Those who do not want to prepare.)
He added that Metro Manila must also have a locally appropriated evacuation plan to address situations when road and communication disruption take place after an earthquake.
"Kaya tayo nag-di-drill para makita yung lapses na itong sector. So yan, inaaral yan," Keyser said.
(We conduct drills to see the lapses of each sector and study it.)

Meanwhile, geologist Charmaine Villamil of the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) explained changes in the climate do not trigger the occurrence of an earthquake but can aggravate its effects.
"Changes in the climate will not trigger the occurrence of earthquake, but the effects of climate change can aggravate the effects of tsunami," Villamil said.
"Kapag dumating yung tsunami, mas mataas pa po yung aasahan na alon," she added.
(Once a tsunami occurs, expect higher waves.)
The United Nation has designated every November 5 as World Tsunami Awareness Day to promote preparedness for natural disasters.
This include urging the public to participate in drills, runs, or walks along tsunami evacuation routes to help build resilience.
For its part, the PHIVOLCS will hold the “Tsunami! Run for Safety: Shake, Drop, or Roar? Move Away from the Shore!” on October 24 in Pasay City. — LA, GMA News

articles.title: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil project

Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests…
articles.byline: Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland islands

blocks.text: Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands.

With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.

A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood that the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands.

An oil project known as Sea Lion in the north Falklands basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.

Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”

It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.

Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

The intensity of the Argentinian menace relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.

Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
after newsletter promotion
A draft national sovereignty introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.

The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.

Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.

In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annexe VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.

On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such a legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.

Under it, Buenos Aires will claim that the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.

At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.

“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”

The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.

A graduate of Central Mindanao University took the top spot in the licensure examination for professional foresters, given earlier this month.

According to the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC), 1,406 test takers out of 1,892 passed the exam, given by the Board for Foresters at test enters in Metro Manila, Baguio, Butuan, Cagayan de Oro, Cebu, Davao, Iloilo, Koronadal, Legazpi, Lucena, Pagadian, Pampanga, Rosales, Tacloban and Tuguegarao.

Joey Siarez Jumawan of Central Mindanao University achieved the highest score of 94.10%, while the top performing school with 50 or more examinees is the University of the Philippines-Los Baños, with all 129 of its test takers passing.

articles.title: Trump targets Ilhan Omar at rally following raid on her home – US politics live
articles.summary: President says Somalia, birthplace of the Minnesota Democratic congresswoman, is ‘one of the worst countries on the planet’

blocks.text: Key events

items: 21m agoCongresswoman Omar says she will 'not be silenced' as Trump targets her at rally following raid

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Monday tried to boost senator Jon Husted’s reelection campaign by attacking two groups of immigrants during a rally in Ohio.

Trump also gave a shoutout to representative Max Miller, the Republican congressman who refused to stop running for reelection after facing accusations of domestic abuse, pointing him out in the audience.
“Thank you, Max, for coming,” Trump said. “Thank you. Very good.”

Trump focused, however, on a favorite issue — immigration. Trump has long targeted Minnesota’s large population of Somali immigrants and on Monday he linked that group to Haitians in Springfield, Ohio.

During a presidential debate two years ago, Trump falsely accused the latter group of eating pets. Referencing those allegations Monday, Trump said “I was right” and boasted that Haitians were being driven out of the country by his administration’s policies .

“If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota is being destroyed, we’re going to stop it,” Trump said. “Just like we did with Springfield, we’re going to stop it, we’re not going to let it happen.”
Congresswoman Omar says she will 'not be silenced' as Trump targets her at rally following raid
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar said she will “not be silenced” and called a search of her Washington home part of President Donald Trump’s “intimidation” campaign.
Democratic representative Omar, an outspoken critic of the president, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican’s “political enemies”.
It comes as Trump targeted the congresswoman during a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, last night. He said Somalia, where Omar was born, is “one of the worst countries ⁠anywhere on the planet”.
He said:
double quotation markShe comes from one of the worst countries ⁠anywhere on the planet. What a mess they have done - Somalia.

He urged supporters to vote Republican “if you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed”. In response, the crowd of Republican supporters chanted: “Deport, deport.”
US authorities conducted a predawn raid of Omar’s home in Washington, DC, on Monday as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said.

A person familiar with the investigation said it is ⁠related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of ⁠the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker’s immigration paperwork filled out ​by her late father when she was a child.
Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president.
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” she said. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

In a statement, US House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party’s leadership in the chamber said the raid was “deeply disturbing and raises serious questions” about the weaponization of the federal government against Trump’s enemies.
In other developments:

items: A federal judge has ordered Donald Trump’s administration to temporarily halt the broadcast of taxpayer-funded television ads promoting the president ahead of the 3 November midterm elections. Effective as of 6.45pm ET on Sunday, US district judge Jennifer L Rochon of the southern district of New York issued a temporary restraining order aimed at the ads that is meant to stay in effect for at least 14 days.

The New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, compared US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)’s recent shooting of a man in the Manhattan enclave of Marble Hill to a mass shooting scene – and called for an end to the agency’s operations in his city. Mamdani’s joined MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff for his first media interview since ICE agents shot and wounded Oscar Belgal, 28, during an enforcement operation while he was in his car with his five-year-old child also inside.

The Republican US senator Roger Marshall says he has finally paid off a bakery debt – after six years and repeated collection attempts reported by a Kansas business that had supplied a large order of treats for a 2020 election watch party. “We have absolutely no idea how this happened”, the Kansas senator wrote in a social media post containing a screenshot of the payment on a $678.75 invoice from Holly’s Sweet Treats as well as his $1,300 payment. “And we have repaid the bill … double.”

A businessman wanted for years in the US for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody. Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro.

articles.title: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
articles.summary: The judge who helped convict Jair Bolsonaro is caught up in a crisis that could benefit his son and damage Lula
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.
“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.

Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.

blocks.caption: Jair Bolsonaro supporters protest against Alexandre de Moraes in São Paulo in September 2024, a month after the supreme court justice ordered X to be suspended in Brazil. Photograph: Jorge Silva/Reuters

blocks.text: Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.

The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.
Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.

The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.

Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”.

Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.

blocks.caption: Lula greets supporters at a campaign rally in Ceilândia this month. The president told the crowd he would win the election and that Brazil would not return to fascism. Photograph: André Borges/EPA

blocks.text: “These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters.

“We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.”

Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”.

The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial.

On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father about the elections that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media.

Beyond the anger of Bolsonaro’s supporters, legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian.
“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes.

While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest.

Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.

Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign.

blocks.caption: Alexandre de Moraes has previously been likened by Elon Musk to the Harry Potter villain Lord Voldemort. Photograph: Carla Carniel/Reuters

blocks.text: Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing.

No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker.

Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date.

blocks.caption: A girl plays with political flyers at the Cidade de Deus favela, in south-west Rio de Janeiro, on polling day. Photograph: Tercio Teixeira/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted.

“With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.”

Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father.
“We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility.
“The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

articles.title: AFP backs Gibo Teodoro amid Chinese Embassy's criticism of severed military dialogue
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday rallied behind Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. after a Chinese Embassy rant on the severed military dialogue…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 5:46pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday rallied behind Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro Jr. after a Chinese Embassy rant on the severed military dialogue between Manila and Beijing.

“The DND’s decision to suspend military-to-military communication channels with PRC, three (3) years ago, was based on experience and the consistent failure of these mechanisms to produce meaningful results amid continued provocative and irresponsible actions by their People’s Liberation Army and China Coast Guard,” the AFP said in a statement.

“Upholding the Constitution and safeguarding our sovereign rights is a duty incumbent upon every Filipino. United as one nation, the Filipino people and the AFP will continue to defend our territorial integrity,” the organization added.
In a statement on Monday, October 12, the Chinese Embassy accused Teodoro of suspending the military-to-military communication between China and Philippines for his “political self interests.”
“Everyone knows that no matter how difficult bilateral relations become, communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating,” the embassy said.

“But Gibo Teodoro decided to shut down mil-mil communication between China and the Philippines for political self interests. His move fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation,” it added.
In response, Teodoro noted that the said dialogue channel between Manila and Beijing was already suspended a long time ago.

“Here we go again… Military-to-military ties have long been suspended—for roughly three years now. They said this again because it's a desperate move on their part—because they were caught in their own 'foolishness’,” he said in Filipino in a Facebook post.

The Defense Dept. also reposted on Facebook the statement released in May 2024, noting the discontinuation of the communications between the department and the Chinese Embassy after Teodoro assumed office in July 2023. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News
